Handling questions from a room of people

switchJobs.title: Accountant or finance analyst
switchJobs.summary: You already work with numbers, spreadsheets and checking that totals reconcile.
strengths: Explaining a result to someone who needs a decision

switchJobs.title: Customer support or success
switchJobs.summary: You already solve problems for real people and write clear answers to them.
strengths: Calm problem-solving with a worried person

switchJobs.title: Nurse or healthcare worker
switchJobs.summary: You already follow careful procedures, record what happened, and stay calm when things go wrong.

switchJobs.title: Graphic or print designer

strengths: Taking feedback and iterating on a design

switchJobs.title: Marketer or content writer

switchJobs.title: Sales or account manager

strengths: Understanding what a customer really needs
Following up and keeping track of many relationships

switchJobs.title: Researcher or scientist

switchJobs.title: Engineer in another field (mechanical or electrical)

switchJobs.title: Office or operations administrator

roles.title: AI Engineer
roles.summary: AI engineers build products on top of large language models - chat assistants, retrieval over company documents, agents that use tools - and make them reliable, safe and affordable in production.
roles.whereTheyWork: AI-first startups, product teams adding AI features at established companies, consultancies, and internal-tools teams automating work with LLMs.
dayInLife: Build a retrieval pipeline so an assistant answers from a company's own documents.
Write and refine a prompt, then prove the change helped with an evaluation set.
Add a tool an agent can call, with guardrails on what it's allowed to do.
Cut cost and latency by caching answers and choosing the right model size.
Investigate a bad answer a user reported and trace where it went wrong.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Strong Python, APIs and the software basics AI work sits on.
stages.project: A Python script that calls a public API, handles errors and retries, and stores results - with tests.
stages.doneWhen: You can build a small, tested Python service that talks to other services over HTTP.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Working with LLMs directly - prompts, structured output and retrieval.
stages.project: A "chat with your docs" app over a set of PDFs that cites the passages it used.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain why an answer was wrong - retrieval, prompt or model - and fix the right part.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Agents, evaluation and shipping it.
stages.project: An agent that completes a real task with two or three tools, plus an evaluation suite that runs in CI and a deployed demo.
stages.doneWhen: You can show, with numbers, that a change made your system better rather than just different.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Reliability, cost and architecture at scale.
stages.project: Write a design doc for an AI feature with latency, cost and failure budgets, and the plan for monitoring quality after launch.
stages.doneWhen: You can choose between prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning and plain code - and justify it.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding in Python - practical rather than puzzle-heavy at many companies
LLM system design - e.g. design a support assistant over a knowledge base
Discussion of a project you built - choices, evaluation and failures
Behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: This role exists because of AI and changes as fast as the models do. Tools and frameworks shift every few months, so the lasting skills are the fundamentals - software engineering, retrieval, evaluation and cost control. Engineers who can measure quality, rather than judge it by eye, are the ones teams trust to ship.

market.text: AI engineer has become one of the fastest-growing job titles since 2023, at both startups and established companies adding AI features.
Postings typically want strong Python and software engineering first, then LLM experience - retrieval, agents and evaluation - shown through projects.

tasteTest.task: Use a free AI model's API or web chat to build a small question-answer tool over three short documents you write yourself, and test five questions.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The tool answers the five questions, and you can name one question it got wrong and say why.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You want to build useful products with AI, and you are curious how models are used in real apps.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to train models yourself or work on the maths inside them.

roles.title: Analytics Engineer
roles.summary: Analytics engineers turn raw data into clean, tested, well-documented tables that analysts and dashboards can trust - applying software engineering habits to SQL and data modelling.
roles.whereTheyWork: Tech and SaaS companies, e-commerce, fintech, and any organisation with a modern data stack (a cloud warehouse plus dbt).
dayInLife: Model raw event data into a clean "orders" table with one row per order.
Add tests so a duplicate in a source system is caught before it reaches a dashboard.
Agree on exactly how "monthly active users" is defined, then encode it once.
Review a teammate's dbt pull request.
Speed up a model that's become slow and expensive.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: SQL in depth and how analysts use data.
stages.project: Answer ten business questions on a public dataset with advanced SQL (CTEs, window functions), all version-controlled in Git.
stages.doneWhen: You can write complex SQL confidently and explain why your numbers are correct.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Modelling and transforming data properly.
stages.project: A dbt project on a warehouse - staging, intermediate and mart layers, with tests and documentation.
stages.doneWhen: Your models have clear grain, tests on every key, and docs someone else can follow.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Shipping data like software, and serving it to people.
stages.project: Run your dbt project in CI, schedule it, and build a dashboard on your marts with documented metric definitions.
stages.doneWhen: A broken change is caught in CI, and analysts self-serve from your models.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Owning the data model and metric definitions for a business.
stages.project: Design a semantic layer or metrics catalogue for a company and the plan to migrate dashboards onto it.
stages.doneWhen: The company trusts one set of numbers - and they come from your models.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Advanced SQL test
Data modelling exercise - design tables for a business process
dbt or take-home project review
Behavioural round on working with analysts and stakeholders

roles.aiImpact: AI can now answer data questions in plain English - but only reliably on top of clean, well-defined, documented models. That makes analytics engineering more important, not less - the semantic layer and metric definitions you build are what AI tools query.

market.text: The analytics engineer title grew with the "modern data stack" - cloud warehouses plus dbt - and is now common at data-mature companies.
Postings almost always ask for strong SQL and dbt; Python and a BI tool are common extras.

tasteTest.task: Write three SQL queries that build one clean summary table from a small set of raw rows, then describe in two sentences what each query is for.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The summary table gives the same answer when you run it twice, and each query has a sentence explaining its purpose.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like SQL and want to define what a business metric means so others can trust it.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to build models or systems from scratch, rather than shape data for others to use.

roles.title: Android Engineer
roles.summary: Android engineers build native apps for the world's most-used mobile platform with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose - fast, reliable apps that work across thousands of device models.
roles.whereTheyWork: Consumer apps, fintech and payments, e-commerce, ride-hailing and delivery, media and streaming, phone makers, and companies with large audiences in markets where Android dominates.
dayInLife: Build a new screen in Jetpack Compose from a Figma design.
Move slow work off the main thread so scrolling stays smooth.
Reproduce a crash that only happens on one manufacturer's phones.
Review how a feature behaves when the app is killed and restored.
Ship a staged rollout on Google Play and watch crash rates.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Kotlin, Git and how apps talk to servers.
stages.project: A Kotlin command-line app (a budget or habit tracker) using data classes, collections, null safety and coroutines.
stages.doneWhen: You're fluent in Kotlin basics, null safety and coroutines, and can solve easy coding problems.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Modern Android UI, architecture and data.
stages.project: A news or recipes app with Compose, a ViewModel, Retrofit for an API, Room for offline data, and dark mode.
stages.doneWhen: Your app survives rotation and process death without losing state, and works offline.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Testing, auth and shipping to Google Play.
stages.project: Publish your app on Google Play (internal testing is fine) with sign-in, unit and UI tests, and a CI build.
stages.doneWhen: Anyone can install your app from a link, and your tests run on every pull request.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Performance, modular architecture and leading a codebase.
stages.project: Profile your app on a low-end phone, fix startup time and jank, and write up the before/after numbers.
stages.doneWhen: You can lead architecture decisions for a multi-module app used by millions.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding - data structures and algorithms, often in Kotlin
Android fundamentals - lifecycle, coroutines, Compose, memory leaks
Live or take-home app exercise
Mobile system design for mid-level and above (e.g. an offline-first chat app)

roles.aiImpact: Android Studio's AI assistant and other tools generate Compose UI and boilerplate quickly. What stays valuable is what's genuinely hard on Android - lifecycle and state across process death, performance on low-end devices, fragmentation across manufacturers, and battery and memory budgets.

market.text: Android has the majority of smartphone users worldwide, which keeps native Android skills in steady demand - especially in markets across Asia, Africa and Latin America.
Kotlin and Jetpack Compose are now Google's recommended way to build Android apps; most new job posts ask for both.

tasteTest.task: Follow an official beginner guide to make a single Android screen that shows a title and a button, and read through what the code does line by line.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The app runs on an emulator or a phone, and you can name the file that holds the screen layout.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You enjoy a clear, step-by-step build and like seeing an app run on a real or virtual phone.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You do not want to install large developer tools, or you dislike long setup steps.

roles.title: Application Security Engineer
roles.summary: Application security engineers find and fix security flaws in the software a company builds - reviewing designs and code, testing for vulnerabilities, and building guardrails so developers ship secure code by default.
roles.whereTheyWork: Tech and SaaS companies, banks and fintech, healthcare, e-commerce, security consultancies, and government and defence contractors.
dayInLife: Threat-model a new payments feature with the team building it.
Review a pull request that changes how sessions work.
Triage findings from a security scanner and separate real risks from noise.
Verify and fix a vulnerability reported through the bug bounty programme.
Add a security check to the CI pipeline so a class of bug can't come back.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: How the web works, one language and solid development basics.
stages.project: Build a small web API with login in Python, then write down every way you think it could be attacked.
stages.doneWhen: You can read and write code comfortably and explain HTTP, cookies and sessions in detail.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Web vulnerabilities and how to find them.
stages.project: Work through the PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs for the main vulnerability classes, and write up five in your own words.
stages.doneWhen: You can find, exploit (in a lab) and explain how to fix each OWASP Top 10 class.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Security in the development lifecycle.
stages.project: Add SAST, dependency and secret scanning to a CI pipeline, threat-model an app, and fix what you find.
stages.doneWhen: You can review a design or pull request and give developers specific, fixable feedback.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Security programmes and architecture.
stages.project: Write a secure-by-default guideline for your stack (auth, secrets, input handling) and get a team to adopt it.
stages.doneWhen: Developers come to you early, and whole classes of vulnerabilities stop appearing.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Web security fundamentals - explain and fix common vulnerabilities
Secure code review - find the bugs in a snippet
Threat modelling or design review exercise
Coding or scripting, and a behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: AI coding tools increase the volume of code shipped - and AI-generated code can repeat insecure patterns confidently. That raises demand for people who can review code, design guardrails and automate checks at scale. AI features also bring new risks, such as prompt injection and data leakage, that AppSec teams now own.

market.text: Application security is one of the most consistently hired specialisms in cybersecurity, especially at companies building their own software.
Postings usually want development experience plus web security knowledge; certifications help less than demonstrable skills (labs, write-ups, bug bounty findings).

tasteTest.task: Read through a simple login form you have built or been given, list three ways it could be attacked, and suggest one fix for each.
tasteTest.doneWhen: Each attack has a plain description and a specific, realistic fix.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You think like someone trying to break things, and you like working out how systems fail safely.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You prefer building features to reviewing how they could be misused.

roles.title: Backend Engineer
roles.summary: Backend engineers build the parts of a product users never see - APIs, databases, authentication, background jobs - and keep them correct, fast and secure as traffic grows.
roles.whereTheyWork: Almost every software company - SaaS, fintech, e-commerce, marketplaces, banks and enterprise IT, and the platform teams inside large tech companies.
dayInLife: Design and build an API endpoint, from the database query to the JSON response.
Write a database migration and check it won't lock a busy table.
Investigate why one request in a hundred is slow, using logs and traces.
Review a pull request for correctness, security and error handling.
Agree on the shape of an API with the frontend and mobile teams.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: One programming language, the tools every engineer uses, and how requests travel.
stages.project: A command-line tool that reads a CSV, transforms it and writes a report - with tests, in a public Git repo.
stages.doneWhen: You can solve easy and some medium coding problems in your language, and explain what happens during an HTTP request.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: APIs and databases - the heart of the job.
stages.project: A REST API for a small product (say, a book club) with sign-up, login, CRUD endpoints, PostgreSQL and automated tests.
stages.doneWhen: You can design tables and endpoints for a new feature on paper, then build them with tests, without a tutorial.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Shipping it, running it and keeping it safe.
stages.project: Containerise your API, deploy it with a CI pipeline, add caching to a slow endpoint, and add logging and a health check.
stages.doneWhen: A push to main runs tests and deploys automatically, and you can find the cause of an error from logs alone.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Systems that scale, and decisions others build on.
stages.project: Write a design doc for a feature that needs a background queue (e.g. sending 100k emails), then build and load-test it.
stages.doneWhen: You can defend trade-offs between consistency, cost and complexity - and you've been on call for something you built.

tools: VS Code or an IDE like PyCharm

rounds: Recruiter or hiring-manager screen
Coding - data structures and algorithms, usually 1–2 problems
Practical backend round - build or extend a small API, or debug one
System design for mid-level and above (e.g. a URL shortener, rate limiter or chat service)
Behavioural round on ownership, incidents and collaboration

roles.aiImpact: AI assistants now write a lot of routine backend code - CRUD endpoints, validation, tests, SQL. The value has shifted to judgement that AI handles poorly - data modelling, knowing what can fail in production, security, and designing systems that stay simple as they grow. Backend engineers also increasingly build the services that call LLM APIs, so knowing how to work with them safely is becoming part of the job.

market.text: PostgreSQL is the most-used database among respondents to recent Stack Overflow Developer Surveys, and Python and JavaScript/TypeScript are among the most-used languages.
Backend job posts commonly ask for one main language (Python, Java, Go, C# or Node.js), SQL, Docker and experience with a cloud provider.

tasteTest.task: Write a tiny program that answers web requests, for example one route that returns today's date as JSON, and call it from your browser.
tasteTest.doneWhen: Your address returns the data, and you can say what happens between your request and the reply.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like logic and data, and you are happy when things work without a screen to look at.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want most of your work to be visible on a screen you can show to people.

roles.title: Cloud Engineer
roles.summary: Cloud engineers design, build and run infrastructure on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud - networks, compute, storage, identity and cost - so applications are secure, reliable and affordable.
roles.whereTheyWork: Companies moving to or running in the cloud, consultancies and managed-service providers, banks and enterprises, and cloud providers themselves.
dayInLife: Set up a new environment - network, database and permissions - with infrastructure as code.
Help a team move an application from on-premise servers to the cloud.
Track down why last month's cloud bill jumped 30%.
Tighten permissions after a security review.
Plan for a region outage and test the recovery steps.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Linux, networking and scripting.
stages.project: Build a small network of two Linux VMs, host a website behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS, and automate setup with a script.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain subnets, DNS and firewalls, and debug connectivity from the terminal.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: One cloud provider, properly.
stages.project: Deploy a three-tier app on AWS (load balancer, app servers, managed database) with least-privilege IAM and a budget alert.
stages.doneWhen: You can design a secure, highly available setup for a typical web app and estimate its monthly cost.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Infrastructure as code, containers and automation.
stages.project: Recreate your setup entirely in Terraform, deployed through a CI pipeline, with monitoring and alerts.
stages.doneWhen: You can tear down and rebuild your environment with one command.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Architecture, cost and governance at scale.
stages.project: Write a migration plan for a legacy app - target architecture, cost estimate, risks and rollback plan.
stages.doneWhen: You can design multi-account, multi-region setups and defend their cost.

tools: Azure or Google Cloud consoles and CLIs

rounds: Recruiter screen
Cloud fundamentals - networking, IAM, storage and compute choices
Scenario questions - design or troubleshoot an architecture
Hands-on task - Terraform, scripting or a broken environment
Behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: AI assistants now draft Terraform, IAM policies and architecture diagrams quickly, but mistakes in cloud configuration are expensive and sometimes public. The value is in reviewing that output - security, cost and failure modes - and in designing architectures that fit the business, which AI can't decide on its own.

market.text: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud together host most cloud workloads; AWS appears most often in job posts, with Azure strong in large enterprises.
Cloud certifications (such as AWS Solutions Architect Associate) are widely requested for these roles and help career changers get interviews.

tasteTest.task: Create a free cloud account and launch one small server or storage bucket, then delete it, noting every step and the cost (zero).
tasteTest.doneWhen: You have launched and removed one resource, with notes on each step in plain words.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like learning how computers are rented, connected and organised across the internet.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You get anxious about configuration screens or prefer hands-off products.

roles.title: Cloud Security Engineer
roles.summary: Cloud security engineers protect a company's cloud accounts, identities, networks and data - designing secure foundations, catching misconfigurations, and responding when something goes wrong.
roles.whereTheyWork: Companies running on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud - especially fintech, healthcare, SaaS and enterprises - plus security consultancies and cloud providers.
dayInLife: Review a Terraform change that opens a database to a new network.
Investigate an alert about unusual access from a service account.
Tighten IAM permissions that grew too broad over time.
Build guardrails that block public storage buckets across every account.
Help a team pass a compliance audit (SOC 2, ISO 27001).

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Linux, networking and how the cloud works.
stages.project: Build and harden a Linux server in the cloud - SSH keys only, firewall, automatic updates - and document every choice.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain networking, encryption basics and how to secure a single server.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Cloud architecture and its security controls.
stages.project: Deploy a small app on AWS with Terraform using least-privilege IAM, private networking and encryption - then threat-model it.
stages.doneWhen: You can design a secure cloud setup and explain the shared-responsibility model.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Detection, automation and containers.
stages.project: Add misconfiguration scanning to a CI pipeline, practise on deliberately vulnerable cloud labs, and write an incident playbook.
stages.doneWhen: You can find and fix common cloud misconfigurations and respond to an alert methodically.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Security architecture across many accounts and teams.
stages.project: Design a multi-account security baseline - identity, logging, guardrails, incident response - as a design doc.
stages.doneWhen: New teams get secure-by-default cloud environments without asking.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Cloud and security fundamentals - IAM, networking, encryption
Scenario - investigate an incident or review an architecture
Hands-on - find misconfigurations in Terraform or a cloud account
Behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: Attackers and defenders both use AI. Security teams use it to triage alerts and review configurations faster, while new AI services add risks such as exposed model endpoints and data leaking into prompts. Engineers who understand cloud fundamentals deeply are needed to judge what AI flags - and what it misses.

market.text: Cloud misconfiguration remains one of the most common causes of breaches, keeping cloud security in steady demand.
Postings often ask for a cloud certification plus a security certification, alongside hands-on Terraform and Kubernetes experience.

tasteTest.task: In a free cloud account, check who has access to what, remove one unnecessary permission, and write down why it was unnecessary.
tasteTest.doneWhen: You have made one real change, and you can explain the risk it removes in one sentence.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like careful, detailed checking, and you enjoy locking down systems so only the right people get in.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to build the apps themselves rather than secure how they are set up.

roles.title: Cross-platform Mobile Engineer
roles.summary: Cross-platform mobile engineers build one app that runs on both iPhone and Android - usually with Flutter or React Native - and get it through the app stores and onto people's phones.
roles.whereTheyWork: Startups and product companies that need both platforms with a small team, agencies building client apps, and fintech, delivery and consumer apps.
dayInLife: Build a new screen from a Figma design and make it feel right on both iOS and Android.
Connect the screen to an API and handle slow networks and offline states.
Chase a crash that only happens on one Android model.
Prepare a release - version numbers, screenshots, store notes - and submit it for review.
Decide whether a feature needs a small piece of native code.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Programming basics in the language your framework uses, plus Git.
stages.project: A small Dart command-line program (a quiz or budget tracker) using classes, lists and async code.
stages.doneWhen: You're comfortable with variables, functions, classes, null safety and async/await in Dart.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Building real screens, navigation and data.
stages.project: A weather or recipes app with several screens, navigation, a live API, loading and error states, and dark mode.
stages.doneWhen: You can build any screen from a design and keep state predictable as the app grows.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Testing, authentication and shipping to both stores.
stages.project: Publish an app to Google Play and the App Store (or TestFlight) with sign-in, tests and a CI build.
stages.doneWhen: A stranger can install your app from a store link - and it doesn't crash.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Performance, native integration and app architecture.
stages.project: Write a small native module (Kotlin or Swift) your Flutter app calls, and add crash reporting and performance monitoring.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain your app's architecture and make it fast on a cheap Android phone.

tools: Xcode (needs a Mac for iOS builds)
an Android phone and an emulator

rounds: Recruiter screen
Language and framework fundamentals (widgets, state, lifecycle, async)
Take-home or live build of a small app screen with an API
Architecture discussion for mid-level and above (state, offline, navigation)
Behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: AI assistants are good at generating widgets and boilerplate, so building a basic screen is no longer a differentiator. Mobile engineers stand out by handling what's genuinely hard on phones - performance on cheap devices, offline behaviour, platform quirks, accessibility and getting through store review.

market.text: Flutter and React Native are the two dominant cross-platform frameworks; both appear among the most-used frameworks in the Stack Overflow Developer Survey.
Many companies hire one cross-platform team instead of separate iOS and Android teams, especially at startup size.

tasteTest.task: Sketch a three-screen phone app on paper or in a free design tool, then list which parts would look the same on iPhone and Android.
tasteTest.doneWhen: You have a clear list of shared parts and a short note on the platform differences you would need to handle.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You want to build phone apps without learning two separate languages from the start.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You have no interest in phones or want to avoid the store and review rules that come with them.

roles.title: Data Analyst
roles.summary: Data analysts answer business questions with data - pulling it with SQL, cleaning it, finding what changed and why, and explaining it in charts and dashboards people actually use.
roles.whereTheyWork: Almost every industry - e-commerce, banking, consulting, healthcare, SaaS, logistics - usually within product, marketing, finance or operations teams.
dayInLife: Answer "why did sign-ups drop last week?" with a SQL query and a chart.
Clean a messy export from a CRM before anyone can trust the numbers.
Build or update a dashboard the sales team checks every morning.
Explain a finding to a manager in two minutes, without jargon.
Agree on exactly how a metric like "active user" is defined.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Spreadsheets, SQL and the basic statistics behind every report.
stages.project: Take a public dataset (e.g. a city's bike-share trips), answer five business questions in SQL, and summarise them in a spreadsheet.
stages.doneWhen: You can write queries with joins, GROUP BY and CTEs, and explain a mean, median and percentage change correctly.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Visualising data and turning numbers into a story.
stages.project: A public dashboard (Power BI or Tableau Public) on a topic you care about, with a one-page written summary of what it shows.
stages.doneWhen: Someone non-technical can read your dashboard and tell you the main takeaway.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Python for analysis, experiments and version control.
stages.project: An analysis notebook that cleans a messy dataset, tests a hypothesis, and ends in a clear recommendation - published on GitHub.
stages.doneWhen: You have three portfolio projects, each with a question, method, result and recommendation.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Owning metrics and shaping how the business uses data.
stages.project: Define the core metrics for a product, document them, and build the clean tables that power them.
stages.doneWhen: Teams come to you to decide what to measure, not just to pull numbers.

tools: an AI assistant for writing queries

rounds: Recruiter screen
SQL test - joins, aggregations, window functions
Case study - interpret a dataset or dashboard and make a recommendation
Spreadsheet or BI exercise
Behavioural round on communicating findings to non-technical people

roles.aiImpact: AI can now write SQL and build first-draft charts from a plain-English question, so pulling numbers alone is less valuable. Analysts who thrive know the business, define metrics carefully, spot when a number is wrong, and explain what it means for a decision. Checking AI-written queries against the data is now part of the job.

market.text: SQL appears in the large majority of data analyst job posts, usually alongside Excel and one BI tool (Power BI or Tableau).
Data analyst is one of the most common entry points into tech for career changers, especially from finance, operations and research.

tasteTest.task: Download a free public dataset (for example a city's bike trips) and answer three questions about it using a spreadsheet, then write two sentences summarising the answer.
tasteTest.doneWhen: Each of your three answers has a number and a sentence that someone who did not do the work can follow.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like finding the answer hidden in a pile of numbers and explaining it simply to someone else.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to build systems or products, rather than answer questions about data others produced.

roles.title: Data Engineer
roles.summary: Data engineers build the pipelines and warehouses that every analyst, data scientist and AI system depends on - moving data reliably from where it's created to where it's useful, clean and on time.
roles.whereTheyWork: Any company with meaningful data - tech, banking, e-commerce, telecom, healthcare, logistics - and data consultancies and cloud providers.
dayInLife: Build a pipeline that loads yesterday's orders into the warehouse by 6 a.m.
Fix a job that failed overnight and backfill the missing day.
Model raw events into clean tables analysts can trust.
Add data-quality tests so a broken source doesn't silently corrupt reports.
Cut the cost of a warehouse query that scans far more data than it needs.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: SQL, Python and the tools of the trade.
stages.project: Load a public dataset into PostgreSQL with a Python script, model it into clean tables, and answer five questions in SQL.
stages.doneWhen: You can write complex SQL (window functions, CTEs) and explain how you designed your tables.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Warehouses, transformations and orchestration.
stages.project: A daily pipeline - extract from an API, load into a warehouse, transform with dbt, orchestrated by Airflow, all in Docker.
stages.doneWhen: Your pipeline runs on a schedule, recovers from failures, and has tests on its outputs.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Scale, streaming and the cloud.
stages.project: Process a dataset too large for pandas with Spark, add a streaming source with Kafka, and deploy it on a cloud provider.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain batch vs streaming trade-offs and run both.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Platforms, cost and governance.
stages.project: Design a data platform for a mid-size company - ingestion, storage, modelling, access control and cost - as a design doc.
stages.doneWhen: Teams trust your data without double-checking it, and your platform's costs are predictable.

rounds: Recruiter screen
SQL - advanced queries, window functions, performance
Python coding - data manipulation and some algorithms
Data modelling exercise - design tables for a business process
Pipeline or data system design for mid-level and above

roles.aiImpact: AI systems are hungry for clean, well-organised data, which has increased demand for data engineering rather than reduced it. AI tools help write SQL and pipeline code, but the hard parts - modelling, reliability, cost control and data quality - still need careful engineers. Many data engineers now also build the pipelines that feed retrieval systems and model training.

market.text: SQL, Python, a cloud warehouse and an orchestrator (usually Airflow) appear in most data engineering job posts; Spark and dbt are close behind.
Demand for data engineers has grown alongside AI, because model quality depends on data quality.

tasteTest.task: Write a short script that reads a CSV file, removes duplicate rows, and saves a cleaned copy.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The cleaned file has fewer rows than the original, and you can say which rows were removed and why.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like building the pipes that move data, and you care that the data arrives correct and on time.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to spend most of your time looking at charts or presenting results.

roles.title: Data Scientist
roles.summary: Data scientists use statistics, experiments and machine learning to explain what drives outcomes and predict what happens next - then turn that into decisions a business can act on.
roles.whereTheyWork: Tech and product companies, banks and insurers, e-commerce, healthcare and pharma, consulting, and research labs.
dayInLife: Design an A/B test and work out how long it must run to be trustworthy.
Build a model to predict which customers are likely to cancel.
Explore a new dataset and find the two variables that actually matter.
Explain to a product manager why a result isn't statistically meaningful yet.
Write the analysis up so others can reproduce it.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Python, SQL and the statistics everything else rests on.
stages.project: Analyse a public dataset in a notebook - clean it, describe it, and test one clear hypothesis.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain p-values, confidence intervals and correlation vs causation without notes.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Working with data at speed and showing what it says.
stages.project: Analyse a (real or simulated) A/B test end to end - sample size, results, uncertainty and a recommendation.
stages.doneWhen: You can take a vague business question and turn it into an analysis plan.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Machine learning you can explain and defend.
stages.project: A churn or price-prediction model with honest evaluation, feature importance and a write-up a manager could follow.
stages.doneWhen: Your portfolio shows two complete projects, from question to recommendation.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Deeper models, production and influence.
stages.project: Take a model to production behind an API and monitor how its performance changes over time.
stages.doneWhen: Your analyses change decisions, and other scientists build on your methods.

rounds: Recruiter screen
SQL and Python coding
Statistics and probability questions
Product or case round - design a metric or an experiment
Machine learning concepts and a take-home project for many roles

roles.aiImpact: LLMs now handle a lot of routine coding and first-pass analysis, and some classic modelling problems are solved by calling a foundation model. What remains hard - and valued - is experimental design, causal reasoning, knowing when a result is noise, and translating findings into decisions. Many data scientists now also evaluate and improve LLM-based features.

market.text: Job titles have split - "product data scientist" roles lean on SQL, statistics and experiments, while "ML-focused" roles overlap with ML Engineer.
Most postings ask for Python, SQL and statistics first; deep learning is usually a plus rather than a requirement.

tasteTest.task: Take a small dataset, ask one question you can test, and run one simple comparison (such as two group averages), noting how confident you are in the result.
tasteTest.doneWhen: You can state the question, the comparison, the result, and one reason the result might be wrong.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You enjoy maths and asking "is this difference real or just noise?".
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You find statistics tiring, or you want to focus on software rather than analysis.

roles.title: Design Engineer
roles.summary: Design engineers work where design meets code - turning ideas into polished, interactive interfaces, building design systems, and prototyping in the browser instead of handing off static mockups.
roles.whereTheyWork: Product companies that compete on experience, developer-tool and design-tool companies, agencies and studios, and design-systems teams at large companies.
dayInLife: Prototype a new interaction directly in code to test how it feels.
Turn a Figma component into a production-ready, accessible React component.
Tune an animation until it feels right at 60 frames per second.
Pair with a designer to adjust spacing and type across a whole product.
Document a design-system component with live examples.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: The web's building blocks, plus a designer's eye.
stages.project: Recreate three interfaces you admire, pixel-for-pixel and responsive, and write what makes each one work.
stages.doneWhen: You can build any layout from a design, and explain hierarchy, spacing and contrast choices.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Components, interaction and accessibility.
stages.project: A small library of interactive components (menu, dialog, tabs, toast) with motion, keyboard support and reduced-motion handling.
stages.doneWhen: Your components feel smooth, work with a keyboard and screen reader, and look right in light and dark themes.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Design systems, performance and shipping.
stages.project: A documented design system with tokens and themes, used in a deployed demo site that scores above 90 in Lighthouse.
stages.doneWhen: Designers can use your components without asking you how, and they stay fast.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Owning the experience across a product.
stages.project: Lead a visual refresh of an existing product - audit, plan, design tokens, rollout - and write it up.
stages.doneWhen: Your taste and standards shape how the whole product looks and feels.

tools: Framer Motion or the Web Animations API

rounds: Recruiter or design-lead screen
Portfolio walkthrough - your process and decisions, not just the result
Live build - recreate a design or an interaction in code
Design critique - improve an existing interface
Behavioural round on working with designers and engineers

roles.aiImpact: AI tools can now turn a screenshot or prompt into working UI, which makes generic interfaces cheap. That increases the value of taste - knowing what makes an interface feel good - and of the details AI often gets wrong, like motion, accessibility and consistency across a product.

market.text: Design engineer has become a recognised title at product-focused companies, especially developer-tool and design-tool companies.
Postings usually ask for strong React and CSS plus a portfolio showing interaction work; formal design training is a plus, not a requirement.

tasteTest.task: Take one screen you use often and rebuild its layout in plain HTML and CSS, changing spacing, colour and type until it reads clearly.
tasteTest.doneWhen: You can explain one change you made and why it makes the page easier to use.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You notice spacing, colour and motion, and you care whether a screen feels right.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You find design feedback frustrating or prefer tasks with a single right answer.

roles.title: Developer Advocate
roles.summary: Developer advocates help developers succeed with a platform - writing tutorials and docs, building demos and sample apps, speaking and streaming, and bringing developer feedback back to the product team.
roles.whereTheyWork: Developer-tool and API companies, cloud providers, AI platforms, open-source foundations, and databases and infrastructure vendors.
dayInLife: Write a tutorial that gets a developer from zero to a working app in fifteen minutes.
Build a sample app showing a new feature.
Answer questions in the community forum and Discord.
Record a short video or give a talk at a meetup.
Tell the product team which API is confusing developers most - with evidence.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Real development skills - you have to be a developer first.
stages.project: Build and publish a small app that uses a public API, with a README good enough that a stranger can run it.
stages.doneWhen: You can build small apps confidently in at least one language and explain your code clearly.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Teaching through writing and building.
stages.project: Publish three tutorials (written or video) on a tool you like, each with working code on GitHub.
stages.doneWhen: People you don't know follow your tutorials successfully - and tell you so.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Community, speaking and product feedback.
stages.project: Give a talk or livestream, contribute to an open-source project's docs, and summarise developer feedback for a tool you use.
stages.doneWhen: You have a body of public work - posts, code, talks - that shows how you teach.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Developer experience strategy.
stages.project: Audit a product's onboarding - time to first success, drop-off points - and propose and measure improvements.
stages.doneWhen: Your work measurably improves how quickly developers succeed with a product.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Review of your public work - posts, videos, talks, code
Technical exercise - build a demo or write a tutorial with the product
Presentation or mock talk
Behavioural round on community and working with product teams

roles.aiImpact: Developers increasingly learn through AI assistants, which are trained on and retrieve from public docs and examples. That shifts DevRel work towards excellent, accurate documentation and samples (which AI tools then repeat), plus the human parts AI can't do - community, trust, talks and honest product feedback.

market.text: Developer relations teams are concentrated at developer-tool, API, cloud and AI companies.
Hiring weighs a public portfolio - tutorials, talks, open-source work - at least as much as interviews.

tasteTest.task: Write a short tutorial that teaches one small concept (for example, what an API is) with a working example, then ask one person to read it and tell you where they got stuck.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The tutorial has a working example, and you have written down the place where your reader got confused.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like teaching, writing and speaking, and you enjoy helping developers get started.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to spend most of your time writing production code rather than explaining it.

roles.title: DevOps Engineer
roles.summary: DevOps engineers automate how software is built, tested, deployed and run - pipelines, containers, cloud infrastructure and monitoring - so teams can ship often without breaking production.
roles.whereTheyWork: Any company running software in the cloud - SaaS, fintech, e-commerce, telecom, consultancies and managed-service providers.
dayInLife: Speed up a CI pipeline that takes 25 minutes so developers stop waiting.
Write infrastructure as code for a new service's database and network.
Respond to an alert, find the cause in the dashboards and write it up.
Upgrade a Kubernetes cluster without downtime.
Help a team containerise their app and deploy it safely.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Linux, the command line, networking and scripting.
stages.project: Set up a Linux server (a cheap VPS or a VM), harden SSH, host a website behind Nginx with HTTPS, and automate setup with a script.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain what happens between a DNS lookup and a page load and debug it from the terminal.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Containers, pipelines and one cloud.
stages.project: A CI/CD pipeline that tests, builds a container and deploys an app to AWS on every push to main.
stages.doneWhen: You can take any small app from a repo to a running, updatable deployment.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Infrastructure as code, orchestration and observability.
stages.project: Provision the whole stack with Terraform, run the app on Kubernetes, and add metrics, logs, dashboards and an alert.
stages.doneWhen: You can destroy and recreate your environment with one command, and you'd notice an outage before users do.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Reliability, cost and platforms other teams build on.
stages.project: Write a runbook and an incident post-mortem, and design a self-service deploy path another team could use.
stages.doneWhen: Other teams ship faster because of what you built, and incidents get shorter.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Linux, networking and troubleshooting questions
Scripting or coding exercise (Bash or Python)
Hands-on task - write a pipeline, Dockerfile or Terraform module
Design discussion - deploy and scale a service, handle an outage

roles.aiImpact: AI assistants now write Dockerfiles, pipeline YAML and Terraform quickly, and are good at explaining unfamiliar errors. That makes understanding - of networks, failure modes, security and cost - more important, because mistakes in infrastructure are expensive and AI output needs careful review before it touches production.

market.text: Kubernetes, Terraform and at least one major cloud (AWS most often) are the most requested skills in DevOps job posts.
Many organisations run containers in production; the CNCF's annual survey tracks cloud-native adoption.

tasteTest.task: Put a small web page into a container (a Docker image) and run it on your machine, then write down the three commands you used.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The page loads at a local address, and anyone with your three commands can do the same.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like automating repetitive work and getting software to ship reliably.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You prefer to design features and screens rather than the systems that run them.

roles.title: Embedded / IoT Engineer
roles.summary: Embedded engineers write the software that runs on hardware - sensors, wearables, cars, medical devices, appliances - where memory is tiny, timing matters and bugs can be physical.
roles.whereTheyWork: Automotive and EV companies, consumer electronics, medical devices, industrial automation, aerospace and defence, telecom, and IoT startups.
dayInLife: Write a driver for a new temperature sensor over I2C.
Debug why a device resets every few hours, using a logic analyser.
Cut power use so a battery lasts a year instead of a month.
Implement a secure over-the-air firmware update.
Work with hardware engineers on a new circuit board.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: C, electronics basics and how computers work at a low level.
stages.project: Write C programs that manipulate bits, pointers and memory directly, and build a simple circuit with an LED and button on a breadboard.
stages.doneWhen: You're comfortable with pointers, memory, bitwise operations, and reading a simple circuit diagram.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Microcontrollers and talking to hardware.
stages.project: A device on an ESP32 or STM32 that reads two sensors over I2C/SPI, shows data on a small display and logs it.
stages.doneWhen: You can read a datasheet and get a new sensor working from scratch.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Real-time systems, connectivity and C++.
stages.project: An IoT device running FreeRTOS that sends data over MQTT to a dashboard, with unit tests for its logic.
stages.doneWhen: Your device runs reliably for days, handles network loss, and you can explain its task timing.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Security, reliability and system architecture.
stages.project: Design firmware architecture for a connected product - boot, updates, security, power and logging - as a design doc.
stages.doneWhen: You can lead firmware for a product that ships to thousands of customers.

rounds: Recruiter screen
C fundamentals - pointers, memory, bit manipulation, volatile
Embedded concepts - interrupts, timers, protocols, RTOS
Practical - debug or write code for a microcontroller scenario
Project deep dive and behavioural round

practice.title: Embedded Systems – Shape the World (free course)

roles.aiImpact: AI assistants help with boilerplate and explaining datasheets, but embedded work depends on details AI often gets wrong - exact register settings, timing, memory limits and hardware quirks. Engineers who can verify against datasheets and debug on real hardware remain essential. "Edge AI" (running small models on devices) is a growing area.

market.text: Embedded engineers are in steady demand across automotive, medical, industrial and consumer electronics, with less hiring volatility than many software roles.
C remains the core language in embedded job posts, with C++ and Rust increasingly common.

tasteTest.task: Wire a light to a small microcontroller board (or simulate one online) and write a program that blinks it at a steady rate you choose.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The light blinks at your chosen rate, and you can say what controls the timing.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like physical things that respond to code, and you enjoy understanding how hardware behaves.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to work only on software with no hardware, or you do not want to deal with wires and parts.

roles.title: Forward Deployed Engineer
roles.summary: Forward deployed engineers work directly with customers to build real solutions on their company's product - understanding the customer's problem, writing the integrations and tools that solve it, and feeding what they learn back to the product team.
roles.whereTheyWork: AI companies and model providers, data and analytics platforms, enterprise software companies, and startups selling complex products to large customers.
dayInLife: Sit with a customer's operations team to understand the process they want to automate.
Build a working prototype on your product with the customer's real data, in days.
Write the integration that connects your platform to their systems.
Explain a technical trade-off to a customer's executive in plain language.
Tell your product team which missing feature is blocking three customers.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Strong general engineering - one language, data and APIs.
stages.project: Build a script that pulls data from two public APIs, joins it in SQL and produces a useful report - documented for a non-technical reader.
stages.doneWhen: You can quickly build small tools that connect systems and explain what they do.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Building full solutions fast, including with AI.
stages.project: A small internal tool with a web UI that uses an LLM to answer questions over a company's documents.
stages.doneWhen: You can go from a vague problem to a working demo in a week.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Customers, deployment and reliability.
stages.project: Find a real person with a real problem, build something that helps them, deploy it, and write up what you learned from their feedback.
stages.doneWhen: You've shipped something a real user relies on and can tell the story of how you understood their needs.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Owning large accounts and shaping the product.
stages.project: Write a solution design for an enterprise rollout - architecture, security, data access, rollout plan and success metrics.
stages.doneWhen: Customers trust you with their hardest problems, and your feedback changes the product roadmap.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding - practical problems, often with messy, realistic data
Decomposition or case round - break down an ambiguous customer problem
Customer role-play or presentation
Behavioural round on ownership, ambiguity and communication

roles.aiImpact: The forward deployed role has grown with AI - companies selling AI models and platforms need engineers who can turn a powerful but general product into something that works for a specific customer. AI tools make FDEs faster at building prototypes; the scarce skills are understanding the customer's problem, judging what's feasible, and earning trust.

market.text: The role was popularised by Palantir and has spread quickly to AI labs and enterprise AI companies since 2024.
Postings typically ask for strong software engineering plus communication and travel; many roles involve working on-site with customers.

tasteTest.task: Pick one real problem a friend or family member has with a computer task, and solve it with a small script or spreadsheet, watching them try it.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The person can use your solution without you, and you have noted one thing that confused them.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You enjoy working directly with people and you like solving their exact problem, not an imagined one.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to spend your days at a desk away from customers.

roles.title: Frontend Engineer
roles.summary: Frontend engineers build everything a user sees and interacts with in a web product - layouts, forms, navigation, animations - and make it fast, accessible and reliable on every screen size.
roles.whereTheyWork: Product companies and SaaS startups, e-commerce, agencies and consultancies, media sites, and internal-tools teams inside large companies.
dayInLife: Turn a design from Figma into a working, responsive screen.
Wire that screen to an API, with loading, empty and error states.
Review a teammate's pull request and an AI assistant's suggested changes.
Track down why a page feels slow on a mid-range Android phone.
Agree with backend engineers on the shape of a new API response.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: How the web works and the three languages every page is made of.
stages.project: A responsive personal site with a contact form, published on your own URL.
stages.doneWhen: You can rebuild a simple page from a screenshot without a tutorial and explain what happens between typing a URL and seeing the page.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Real applications - components, types and data from APIs.
stages.project: A job board that loads listings from a public API, with search, filters, loading and error states, fully usable with only a keyboard.
stages.doneWhen: You can design a component tree for a new screen and explain where each piece of state lives and why.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: The tools and habits teams expect on day one.
stages.project: A full app with sign-in, a database-backed feature, automated tests in CI, and a Lighthouse mobile score above 90.
stages.doneWhen: Someone can clone your repo, run one command, and see tests pass - and your live app holds up on a slow phone.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Owning architecture, quality and other people's growth.
stages.project: Lead a feature across teams - write the design doc, set the performance budget, and mentor someone through it.
stages.doneWhen: Other engineers come to you for frontend architecture decisions, and your decisions hold up a year later.

rounds: Recruiter or hiring-manager screen
JavaScript and web fundamentals (closures, the event loop, the DOM, CSS layout)
A live UI build - usually React, sometimes plain JavaScript
Frontend system design for mid-level roles and above (e.g. design an infinite feed or autocomplete)
Behavioural round on collaboration, ownership and trade-offs

roles.aiImpact: AI coding assistants now produce first drafts of components, styles and tests in seconds, so the bar for entry-level work has moved up. What stays valuable is judgement - knowing whether generated UI is accessible, fast and maintainable, structuring state so features don't collide, and turning vague product requirements into clear interfaces. Learn to use these tools daily, and learn the fundamentals well enough to catch their mistakes.

market.text: JavaScript and TypeScript are consistently among the most-used languages in the Stack Overflow Developer Survey, and React remains the most-used web framework there.
Most frontend postings now ask for TypeScript and at least one meta-framework such as Next.js, alongside React.

tasteTest.task: Build one web page with a heading, a short list and a button that changes the page when clicked, using only a text editor and a browser.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The button changes something on the screen, and you can explain in one sentence what the browser did when you clicked it.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You enjoy seeing what you build appear on screen straight away, and you notice when spacing or text looks off.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You would rather work on what happens on a server or in a database, out of sight.

roles.title: Full-Stack Engineer
roles.summary: Full-stack engineers ship features end to end - the screen a user sees, the API behind it and the database underneath - and are trusted to take an idea from sketch to production.
roles.whereTheyWork: Startups and small product teams above all, plus agencies, internal-tools teams and product squads at larger companies.
dayInLife: Build a feature across the stack - a database column, an API route and the form that uses it.
Decide whether logic belongs on the server or in the browser.
Fix a bug a customer reported, starting from a screenshot.
Set up a preview deployment so the designer can try a change.
Review AI-generated code for edge cases before merging it.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: How the web works and the languages every web page is made of.
stages.project: A responsive multi-page site with a working contact form, published on your own domain.
stages.doneWhen: You can build a layout from a screenshot and explain the request–response cycle.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: A frontend framework, a backend runtime and a database - connected.
stages.project: A small product (a habit tracker or job board) with a React frontend, a Node.js API and PostgreSQL.
stages.doneWhen: You can add a feature that needs a new table, a new endpoint and a new screen without help.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: The framework, auth, testing and deployment teams expect.
stages.project: Rebuild your product in Next.js with sign-in, tests in CI and a production deploy with a custom domain.
stages.doneWhen: Your app is live, tested and observable - and you can explain every part of it in an interview.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Architecture, performance and leading features across teams.
stages.project: Take a slow page from your app to a Lighthouse score above 90 and write up what you changed and why.
stages.doneWhen: Teammates ask you how a feature should be split between client, server and database.

rounds: Recruiter or founder screen
Coding - algorithms, or a practical exercise in JavaScript/TypeScript
Take-home or live build of a small full-stack feature
System design for mid-level and above
Behavioural round on shipping, trade-offs and working with product and design

roles.aiImpact: AI tools make one person much faster across the whole stack, which plays to full-stack strengths - small teams can ship what used to take several specialists. The flip side is that shallow knowledge is easier to replace. Aim for depth in at least one layer, and the judgement to check AI output where layers meet - auth, data integrity and error handling.

market.text: Startups and small teams hire full-stack engineers heavily because one person can own a whole feature.
React with TypeScript on the frontend and Node.js or Python on the backend is the most common pairing in full-stack job posts.

tasteTest.task: Make a small page that saves one piece of text (for example a note) and shows it again after you reload the page.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The note survives a reload, and you can point to where it is stored and how the page gets it back.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like building both the screen and the part that stores the data, and you do not mind switching between them.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to go deep on one area, such as only the visuals or only the servers.

roles.title: Game Developer
roles.summary: Game developers program the systems that make games work - gameplay, physics, AI, input, UI and performance - usually with engines like Unity, Unreal or Godot.
roles.whereTheyWork: Game studios of every size, mobile game companies, indie teams, and simulation, training and XR companies.
dayInLife: Implement a new gameplay mechanic from a designer's spec.
Tune character movement until it feels responsive.
Profile a level that drops below 60 frames per second and fix it.
Fix a physics bug where players fall through the floor.
Prototype an idea in a day to see if it's fun.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Programming, maths and game loops.
stages.project: Make a complete tiny game (Pong, Snake or Flappy Bird) from scratch, with a start screen, scoring and game over.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain the game loop, vectors and basic collision, and finish a small game.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: A game engine, properly.
stages.project: A small 2D or 3D game in Unity with several levels, enemies, sound, menus and save data - published on itch.io.
stages.doneWhen: You can build gameplay systems in an engine without following a tutorial step by step.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Performance, C++ and teamwork.
stages.project: Join a game jam with a team, ship a game in a weekend, and profile and optimise one of your projects.
stages.doneWhen: Your portfolio has two or three finished, playable games and you can talk through their code.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Engine and systems depth.
stages.project: Build a reusable system (dialogue, inventory, networking) used across projects, with documentation.
stages.doneWhen: You design core systems others on the team build on.

tools: Unity (C#) or Unreal Engine (C++) or Godot

rounds: Recruiter screen
Portfolio review - playable games you made and the code behind them
Coding - C# or C++, maths and algorithms
Engine-specific questions or a take-home gameplay task
Behavioural round on teamwork and finishing projects

roles.aiImpact: AI tools now help with code, placeholder art and prototyping, letting small teams build more. Finished, polished, fun games still depend on game-feel, performance and design judgement - and a portfolio of shipped games remains the strongest signal for hiring.

market.text: The games industry is competitive and hiring is cyclical; a portfolio of finished, playable games matters more than credentials.
Unity (C#) dominates mobile and indie games; Unreal (C++) dominates high-end console and PC titles.

tasteTest.task: Make a tiny game in a free engine or in the browser where one object moves when you press an arrow key and stops at the edge of the screen.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The object moves, stops at the edge, and you can name the part of the code that handles the key press.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You love games and enjoy seeing a small world react to what you do.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You find long games and creative iteration tiring, or you dislike repeated testing.

roles.title: iOS Engineer
roles.summary: iOS engineers build native apps for iPhone and iPad with Swift and SwiftUI - polished, fast apps that follow Apple's design conventions and pass App Store review.
roles.whereTheyWork: Consumer apps, fintech, health and fitness, media, productivity tools, agencies, and companies whose customers skew towards iPhone.
dayInLife: Build a screen in SwiftUI that adapts to every iPhone size and Dynamic Type setting.
Use async/await to load data without freezing the interface.
Track down a memory leak with Instruments.
Adopt a new iOS feature such as widgets or Live Activities.
Prepare a TestFlight build and respond to App Store review feedback.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Swift, Git and the basics of networking.
stages.project: Solve twenty small problems in Swift Playgrounds or Xcode - optionals, structs, enums, protocols and closures.
stages.doneWhen: You're comfortable with optionals, value vs reference types, protocols and async/await.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: SwiftUI, app architecture and data.
stages.project: A multi-screen SwiftUI app with navigation, a live API, SwiftData for offline storage and full VoiceOver support.
stages.doneWhen: You can build any screen from a design, keep state predictable, and support Dynamic Type and dark mode.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Testing, sign-in and shipping to the App Store.
stages.project: Ship your app on TestFlight (or the App Store) with Sign in with Apple, unit and UI tests, and an automated build.
stages.doneWhen: Strangers can install your app, and it passes App Store review.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Performance, architecture and platform depth.
stages.project: Profile launch time and scrolling with Instruments, fix the worst issues, and document the architecture of your app.
stages.doneWhen: You can design a modular app architecture and mentor others through Apple's platform changes each year.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding - algorithms, often in Swift
iOS fundamentals - memory management, concurrency, SwiftUI state
Take-home or live app exercise
Mobile system design for mid-level and above

roles.aiImpact: Xcode and other assistants now complete Swift and SwiftUI code well, so writing views is less of a differentiator. What stands out is platform depth - concurrency correctness, performance, accessibility, privacy rules and keeping up with Apple's yearly changes - plus the taste to make apps feel native.

market.text: iOS users tend to spend more in apps, so many consumer and subscription businesses invest heavily in native iOS teams.
SwiftUI is Apple's recommended UI framework; most new iOS job posts expect it alongside UIKit knowledge for older code.

tasteTest.task: Follow an official beginner tutorial to build a small iPhone screen with one list and one button, and change the colour of the button.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The app runs in the simulator, and you can explain what the button does when tapped.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like polished, visual apps and you want to build for iPhone specifically.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You do not own a Mac or do not want to work inside Apple's tools.

roles.title: ML Engineer
roles.summary: ML engineers train, deploy and maintain machine learning models in real products - building the data pipelines, training jobs and serving systems that keep models accurate and fast.
roles.whereTheyWork: Tech companies with ranking, search, recommendations or fraud problems; AI labs; autonomous systems and robotics; fintech; and healthcare imaging.
dayInLife: Build features from raw event data for a recommendation model.
Train a model, compare it to the current one and decide if it's worth shipping.
Put a model behind an API and get its response time under budget.
Investigate why a model's accuracy dropped after a product change.
Automate retraining so the model stays fresh without manual work.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Python, the maths behind models, and software basics.
stages.project: Implement linear regression and gradient descent from scratch in NumPy, then compare with scikit-learn.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain what a gradient is and why it's used, and write clean, tested Python.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Classical ML and deep learning, done properly.
stages.project: Train an image or text classifier in PyTorch with a proper validation set, error analysis and a written evaluation.
stages.doneWhen: You can diagnose overfitting, data leakage and class imbalance, and fix them.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Getting models into production and keeping them there.
stages.project: Serve your model behind an API in a container, with a scheduled retraining pipeline and monitoring for drift.
stages.doneWhen: Your model runs in production-like conditions and you'd know within a day if it degraded.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: ML systems at scale.
stages.project: Design an end-to-end ML system (e.g. feed ranking) - data, training, serving, evaluation and cost - as a design doc.
stages.doneWhen: You can make trade-offs between model quality, latency and cost and explain them to non-ML engineers.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding - data structures and algorithms
ML fundamentals - bias/variance, metrics, model choices
ML system design - e.g. design a recommendation or fraud-detection system
Project deep dive and behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: Foundation models have replaced many custom models for language and vision tasks, so some ML work has moved to fine-tuning, evaluation and serving large models efficiently. Demand stays strong for engineers who understand training deeply and can run models reliably and cheaply at scale.

market.text: ML engineer postings increasingly overlap with AI engineering - fine-tuning, serving and evaluating large models alongside classical ML.
Most roles expect solid software engineering; strong coding often matters as much as maths in interviews.

tasteTest.task: Train a simple model on a small public dataset using a notebook, then measure how well it predicts on data it has not seen.
tasteTest.doneWhen: You have one accuracy number on held-out data, and you can say whether it is good enough for the job.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like building models and checking whether they really work on new data.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to focus on the product or on talking with customers, rather than on training models.

roles.title: MLOps Engineer
roles.summary: MLOps engineers build the platform that trains, deploys, serves and monitors machine learning models - so data scientists and ML engineers can ship models reliably, reproducibly and at reasonable cost.
roles.whereTheyWork: Companies running many models in production, AI labs and AI-first startups, cloud providers, and platform teams at large enterprises.
dayInLife: Build a pipeline that retrains a model weekly and only promotes it if it beats the current one.
Get a model's serving latency under 100 ms on cheaper hardware.
Set up monitoring that alerts when input data starts drifting.
Help a data scientist turn a notebook into a reproducible training job.
Manage GPU capacity and cost across teams.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Software engineering, Linux and ML basics.
stages.project: Train a scikit-learn model, then turn the notebook into a tested Python package with a command-line entry point.
stages.doneWhen: You write clean, tested Python and understand how a model is trained and evaluated.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Containers, pipelines and the cloud.
stages.project: A containerised training pipeline with experiment tracking and a model registry, triggered by CI.
stages.doneWhen: Anyone can reproduce any model you've trained from a commit and a run ID.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Serving, scaling and monitoring.
stages.project: Serve a model on Kubernetes with autoscaling, a canary rollout, and drift and latency monitoring.
stages.doneWhen: You can ship a new model version with no downtime and roll back in a minute.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: ML platforms for many teams.
stages.project: Design an internal ML platform - training, feature storage, serving, monitoring and cost controls - as a design doc.
stages.doneWhen: Other teams ship models faster and more safely because of your platform.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding - Python and some algorithms
ML fundamentals - training, evaluation, common failure modes
ML platform or system design - serving, retraining, monitoring at scale
Infrastructure scenario and behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: Large language models have created a new branch of the job - LLMOps - covering prompt and model versioning, evaluation pipelines, GPU serving and inference cost. Demand for engineers who can run AI reliably and cheaply in production has grown sharply.

market.text: MLOps roles overlap with platform and ML engineering; postings most often ask for Kubernetes, a cloud ML platform and Python.
Serving and evaluating large language models has become a growing part of MLOps work since 2024.

tasteTest.task: Take a small model script and put it under version control, with a README that lets someone else run it and get the same result.
tasteTest.doneWhen: A second person (or a fresh folder) can run the script and get the same output.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You care about making systems repeatable, and you find it satisfying when others can run your work without help.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to invent new models rather than keep existing ones running reliably.

roles.title: Platform Engineer
roles.summary: Platform engineers build the internal platform other engineers ship on - golden paths for creating, deploying and running services - so product teams move fast without each reinventing infrastructure.
roles.whereTheyWork: Mid-size and large tech companies with many engineering teams, SaaS providers, banks modernising their engineering, and developer-tool companies.
dayInLife: Build a template that creates a new service with CI, monitoring and deploys already wired up.
Run a survey to find what slows developers down most.
Upgrade the shared Kubernetes platform without disrupting a hundred services.
Write a CLI tool that replaces a ten-step manual process.
Document a golden path and help a team adopt it.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Linux, networking and a systems language.
stages.project: Write a small CLI tool in Go that automates something you do often, with tests and a release build.
stages.doneWhen: You can write and ship a reliable command-line tool, and debug systems from the terminal.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Containers, orchestration and infrastructure as code.
stages.project: A Kubernetes cluster provisioned with Terraform, with a CI/CD pipeline that deploys a sample service on every merge.
stages.doneWhen: You can provision, deploy and upgrade a containerised platform from code alone.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Building a product for developers.
stages.project: A self-service golden path - one command creates a new service with CI, deploys, dashboards and docs.
stages.doneWhen: Someone else can create and deploy a production-ready service using only your docs.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Platform strategy, reliability and adoption.
stages.project: Write a platform roadmap based on developer feedback, with adoption and reliability metrics.
stages.doneWhen: Teams choose your platform because it's genuinely the easiest way to ship.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding - often in Go or Python
Kubernetes, infrastructure and troubleshooting questions
Platform design - e.g. design a self-service deployment system
Behavioural round on working with internal "customers"

roles.aiImpact: AI coding assistants change what developers need from a platform - fast, safe environments to run and verify generated code, and guardrails on what can reach production. Platform teams increasingly provide AI tooling, model access and evaluation infrastructure as part of the internal platform.

market.text: Platform engineering grew out of DevOps as companies scaled; many DevOps roles have been renamed or reorganised into platform teams.
Kubernetes, Terraform, a CI/CD system and a programming language (often Go or Python) are the most common requirements.

tasteTest.task: Write a short guide that lets a teammate deploy a small app to a test environment without asking you, with one command and clear steps.
tasteTest.doneWhen: A friend follows your guide, deploys the app, and does not need to ask you anything.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like making other engineers faster, and you enjoy writing tools and paths that others use.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You want to build customer-facing features rather than the tools behind them.

roles.title: QA Engineer / SDET
roles.summary: QA engineers and SDETs make sure software works before users find out it doesn't - designing what to test, automating those tests, and building the tooling that lets teams release with confidence.
roles.whereTheyWork: Product companies, banks and insurers, healthcare and regulated industries, e-commerce, gaming, and IT services firms.
dayInLife: Read a new feature's requirements and work out the cases most likely to break.
Write automated end-to-end tests for a checkout flow.
Investigate a flaky test that fails one run in ten.
Test an API directly to check errors and edge cases.
Sign off a release - or explain clearly why it shouldn't go out yet.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: How software is built and how testing fits in, plus one language.
stages.project: Write a test plan and 30 test cases for a real website (e.g. a store's checkout), and file well-written bug reports.
stages.doneWhen: You can design boundary, negative and edge cases for any form and explain why each matters.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Automating tests for web apps and APIs.
stages.project: An automated suite for a demo site - UI tests with Playwright and API tests - running locally with a readable report.
stages.doneWhen: Your tests are stable, readable and fail with messages that point to the problem.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Tests in pipelines, at scale, across browsers.
