stages.project: Run your suite in GitHub Actions on every pull request, across browsers, with a load test for one key endpoint.
stages.doneWhen: A failing test blocks a bad merge automatically, and you can say how much traffic the app handles.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Owning quality strategy across teams.
stages.project: Write a test strategy for a product - what to automate, at which level, and what to monitor in production.
stages.doneWhen: Teams ask you how to test something before they build it.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Test design - "how would you test this login page / lift / API?"
Coding - automation code and some easy algorithm problems for SDET roles
Practical - write or fix automated tests
Behavioural round on handling bugs and release pressure

roles.aiImpact: AI tools can now generate test cases and automation code quickly, which shifts value from writing scripts to deciding what's worth testing, building reliable test infrastructure, and testing AI features themselves - where outputs vary and "correct" is harder to define. Testers with strong automation and engineering skills are in a much better position than purely manual testers.

market.text: Postings increasingly ask for automation and coding skills (SDET) rather than manual testing alone; Playwright has become a leading choice for new web automation.
Regulated industries - banking, healthcare, insurance - continue to hire dedicated QA teams.

tasteTest.task: Write five automated tests for a simple web form, including two that try to break it with bad input, and run them.
tasteTest.doneWhen: All five tests run, and at least one of them catches a real problem you could describe.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You enjoy finding what is broken, and you are good at thinking of the case nobody planned for.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You find repeating checks boring, or you want to build the product rather than test it.

us.title: Software quality assurance analysts and testers

roles.title: Site Reliability Engineer
roles.summary: Site reliability engineers keep production systems fast and available - measuring reliability with SLOs, automating away toil, leading incident response and engineering systems so failures are rare and boring.
roles.whereTheyWork: Large-scale tech companies, SaaS providers, fintech and payments, gaming, streaming, and any company where downtime costs real money.
dayInLife: Review the error budget and decide whether a risky launch can go ahead.
Lead the response to an outage, then write a blameless post-mortem.
Automate a manual task the on-call team does every week.
Load-test a service before a big marketing event.
Work with developers to make a service fail gracefully when a dependency is down.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Linux, networking, programming and scripting.
stages.project: Write a Python tool that checks a list of websites, measures response times and alerts you when one is slow or down.
stages.doneWhen: You can debug a slow or failing service from the command line and write solid automation in Python.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Running services - containers, cloud and observability.
stages.project: Run a small service on Kubernetes with metrics, logs, traces, a dashboard and SLO-based alerts.
stages.doneWhen: You can tell from your dashboards whether users are having a good experience - and get alerted when they aren't.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Incidents, capacity and automation.
stages.project: Break your service on purpose (chaos test), respond using a runbook, and write a blameless post-mortem with action items.
stages.doneWhen: You've been on call for something real and improved it afterwards.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Reliability by design across many systems.
stages.project: Write a reliability review of a system - failure modes, SLOs, capacity plan and the three highest-value fixes.
stages.doneWhen: Teams design for reliability from the start because of the practices you set.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding - practical scripting and some algorithms
Linux and networking troubleshooting
Non-abstract large system design - design for reliability and scale with real numbers
Incident scenario and behavioural round

roles.aiImpact: AI is starting to help with incident triage - summarising alerts, searching logs and suggesting likely causes. That speeds up response but doesn't replace judgement under pressure, deep systems knowledge or the engineering work that prevents incidents. SREs are also increasingly responsible for the reliability and cost of AI services themselves.

market.text: SRE practices from Google's SRE books - SLOs, error budgets and blameless post-mortems - are now widely adopted beyond Google.
Most SRE roles expect strong Linux, Kubernetes and a programming language, with on-call experience valued highly.

tasteTest.task: Make a small web app and write a one-page note of what you would check if it started failing at night: what you would measure, and who you would tell.
tasteTest.doneWhen: Your note lists at least three things to check and a clear order to check them in.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You stay calm in a crisis, and you enjoy finding what is actually broken.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You do not want to be on call, or you prefer work with no pressure to keep things running.

roles.title: Solutions Engineer
roles.summary: Solutions engineers show customers how a technical product solves their problem - running demos, designing integrations, answering hard technical questions, and helping customers succeed after they buy.
roles.whereTheyWork: SaaS and developer-tool companies, cloud providers, data and AI platforms, cybersecurity vendors, and enterprise software companies.
dayInLife: Run a tailored demo for a prospect's engineering team.
Design how the product fits into a customer's existing systems.
Build a small proof of concept with the customer's data.
Answer a security questionnaire and an architecture deep-dive.
Bring customer feedback to the product team.

stages.name: Foundations
stages.summary: Broad technical literacy - APIs, data and one language.
stages.project: Build a script that pulls data from a public API, transforms it, and loads it into a database - then explain it to a non-technical friend.
stages.doneWhen: You can explain APIs, databases and authentication clearly to both engineers and executives.

stages.name: Core
stages.summary: Integrations, architecture and the cloud.
stages.project: Integrate two SaaS products through their APIs and OAuth, deploy it, and write the setup guide a customer would follow.
stages.doneWhen: You can design and explain an integration between your product and a customer's systems.

stages.name: Job-ready
stages.summary: Demos, proofs of concept and AI.
stages.project: Record a five-minute demo of a product you like, tailored to a specific customer persona, and build a small proof of concept.
stages.doneWhen: You can run a clear, confident demo and handle questions you didn't expect.

stages.name: Senior
stages.summary: Complex deals and strategic accounts.
stages.project: Write a solution architecture for an enterprise customer - integration, security, data flow and rollout plan.
stages.doneWhen: You lead the technical side of large deals and shape what the product builds next.

rounds: Recruiter screen
Technical discussion - APIs, integrations and architecture
Mock demo or presentation to a panel playing the customer
Case study - design a solution for a customer scenario
Behavioural round on communication and handling objections

roles.aiImpact: AI helps solutions engineers prepare faster - researching customers, drafting answers and building quick prototypes. The human parts - understanding a customer's real situation, building trust and judging what will actually work - matter more as products (especially AI products) get more complex.

market.text: Solutions and sales engineering is a well-paid route for engineers who enjoy people, often with a mix of salary and commission.
AI and data platforms in particular hire solutions engineers who can build quick proofs of concept on customer data.

tasteTest.task: Take one product (a free tool you use) and write a one-page explanation of how it would solve a specific problem for a small business.
tasteTest.doneWhen: The explanation names the problem, the steps to solve it, and one limit of the product.
tasteTest.forYouIf: You like explaining technology to people who are not technical, and you enjoy helping someone choose the right tool.
tasteTest.notForYouIf: You prefer deep technical work over conversations with people.

skills.title: A/B Testing & Experiments
skills.brief: Running controlled experiments - showing two versions to random groups of users - to find out whether a change actually caused an improvement.

learn.detail: Decide what you expect to change, and one primary metric, before starting.
Why random assignment lets you claim cause, not just correlation.
How many users you need to detect the effect you care about.
What a p-value does and doesn't tell you.
Peeking early, testing many metrics, novelty effects and sample ratio mismatch.
Make sure a win on one metric isn't a loss somewhere else.
Effect size with uncertainty, and a clear recommendation.

skills.analogy: An A/B test is a fair taste test in a restaurant. Half the diners get the old recipe and half get the new one, so any difference in what they order comes from the recipe.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a quick comparison of two weeks. It needs enough people and a fixed plan to be trusted.

skills.title: Web Accessibility
skills.brief: Building interfaces everyone can use - including people using screen readers, keyboards, zoom or voice control. It's a legal requirement in many places and simply good engineering.

learn.detail: Use button, nav, main, label and headings properly - most accessibility comes free.
Everything works with Tab, Enter, Space and Escape, with a visible focus ring.
Accessible names, alt text, and announcing changes with live regions.
WCAG contrast ratios - 4.5:1 for body text - and never colour alone.
Use ARIA only when HTML can't express it; wrong ARIA is worse than none.
Labels, error messages and instructions that are announced.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion and support 200% zoom.
Lighthouse and axe, then real keyboard and screen-reader checks.

skills.analogy: Accessibility is like building a shop with a ramp as well as stairs. The ramp is for wheelchairs, but also for the pram and the suitcase, so everyone gets in.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not an extra for a few users. It makes the site better for almost everyone.

skills.title: AI Agents & Tool Use
skills.brief: Agents are LLM systems that take actions - calling tools and APIs in a loop to complete a task. Building them well means knowing when to use them, and keeping them safe and testable.

learn.detail: Fixed steps you control, or a model deciding the next step - start with the simplest that works.
Define tools with clear names, descriptions and input schemas.
Think, act, observe, repeat - and how to stop.
A standard way to connect models to tools and data sources.
What the agent should remember within and across tasks.
Permissions, confirmations for risky actions and limits on cost and steps.
Test on realistic tasks and inspect the full trace, not just the final answer.

skills.analogy: An agent is like a capable assistant with a phone and a to-do list. It tries a step, checks the result, and chooses the next step until the task is done or it gets stuck.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a model that acts on its own forever. It needs limits, checks and a way to stop.

skills.title: Working with AI Coding Tools
skills.brief: Using AI assistants - chat, autocomplete and coding agents - to write, explain and review code faster, while checking their output like you'd check a junior colleague's.

learn.detail: Inline autocomplete, chat in the editor, and agents that edit many files and run commands.
Point the tool at the right files, explain the goal and constraints, and share error messages in full.
Read every change. Check edge cases, security, performance and whether it fits the codebase.
Ask for one change at a time and commit often, so mistakes are easy to undo.
Have tests that tell you when generated code breaks something.
Ask it to explain code and concepts - then verify against official docs.
Know what your tool sends where, and never paste keys or customer data.

skills.analogy: An AI coding tool is like a very fast junior developer who drafts code for you. You still read the draft, test it and decide whether it is right.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a replacement for understanding the code. The tool can be confidently wrong.

skills.title: Workflow Orchestration (Airflow)
skills.brief: Orchestrators schedule and run data and ML pipelines - handling dependencies, retries and monitoring. Apache Airflow is the most widely used.

learn.detail: Pipelines as directed acyclic graphs of tasks, written in Python.
Run hourly, daily or when data arrives.
Run SQL, Python, Spark or containers as steps.
Make tasks idempotent so reruns are safe.
Re-run history after fixing a bug.
See failed runs, logs and alerts in the UI.
Dagster and Prefect take different approaches worth knowing.

skills.analogy: Airflow is the kitchen timer and the head chef's plan. It knows which step must finish before the next, and it tries again when a step burns.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the data itself. It schedules and watches the steps that move the data.

skills.title: API Testing
skills.brief: Testing APIs directly - status codes, response shapes, errors, auth and edge cases - which is faster and more stable than testing everything through the UI.

learn.detail: Most business logic lives behind the API; tests here are fast and stable.
Correct status, headers and body for valid requests.
Missing fields, wrong types and helpful error messages.
No token, expired token, wrong user.
Validate responses against an OpenAPI or JSON schema.
Create and clean up data so tests don't depend on each other.
Postman/Bruno collections, or code with Playwright, pytest or REST Assured.

skills.analogy: Testing an API is like checking a vending machine from the outside. You press a code and check the item, the change and the error message when the code is wrong.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not testing the screen. It checks the service that the screen talks to.

skills.title: Publishing to App Stores
skills.brief: Getting an app onto Google Play and the Apple App Store - signing, builds, store listings, privacy details, review guidelines and release tracks.

learn.detail: Google Play Console and the Apple Developer Program (paid yearly).
Android app bundles and keystores; iOS certificates and provisioning.
Name, description, screenshots and keywords that help people find you.
Privacy policy, data-safety forms and permission explanations.
Common rejection reasons and how to avoid them.
TestFlight and Play internal/closed testing before release.
Versioning, staged rollouts and responding to reviews.

resources.title: Play Console: Create and set up your app
Flutter: Build and release an Android app
Flutter: Build and release an iOS app

skills.analogy: Publishing an app is like getting a product onto a shop shelf. You need the right packaging, a signed label, a description and a check that it meets the shop's rules.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just uploading a file. Each store has its own review and privacy rules.

skills.title: Authentication & Authorization
skills.brief: Authentication proves who a user is; authorisation decides what they're allowed to do. Getting both right is what keeps accounts and data safe.

learn.detail: Who are you? vs what can you do?
Hash with bcrypt or Argon2. Never store or log plain text.
Server-side sessions with secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies.
Stateless tokens - what's inside, how they're signed, and their pitfalls.
'Sign in with Google' - delegated login without handling passwords.
Role-based access control, and checking permissions on the server every time.
When to use Supabase Auth, Auth0, Clerk or Firebase instead of building it.
MFA, password reset flows and email verification.

skills.analogy: Authentication is showing your ID at the door to prove who you are. Authorisation is what the bouncer lets you do once you are inside, such as VIP areas or staff rooms.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the same as permissions. Knowing who someone is does not tell you what they may do.

skills.title: AWS
skills.brief: Amazon Web Services is the largest cloud platform. Learn the core building blocks - compute, storage, databases, networking and identity - and how to run apps on them safely and affordably.

learn.detail: Users, roles and policies - least privilege from day one.
EC2 virtual machines, Lambda functions and container services (ECS, EKS).
S3 for files, EBS for disks, and lifecycle rules to control cost.
RDS for PostgreSQL/MySQL and DynamoDB for key-value data.
VPCs, subnets, security groups, load balancers and Route 53.
CloudWatch metrics, logs and alarms.
Budgets, alerts and turning things off.
AWS's own checklist for reliable, secure, efficient systems.

skills.analogy: AWS is a huge warehouse-and-utilities company for computing. You rent the storage, power and delivery you need, and pay for what you use instead of building your own depot.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a single service. It is hundreds of services, and you start with a handful.

skills.title: BI Tools (Power BI, Tableau, Looker)
skills.brief: Business intelligence tools turn data into interactive dashboards that teams check every day. Power BI and Tableau are the most requested in analyst job posts.

learn.detail: Import from spreadsheets, databases and warehouses; know live vs extract.
Relationships, fact and dimension tables, and avoiding double counting.
DAX in Power BI or calculated fields in Tableau.
One question per view, filters that make sense, nothing decorative.
Filters, drill-downs and tooltips that help people explore.
Publish, schedule refreshes and manage who sees what.
Keep dashboards fast as data grows.

skills.analogy: A BI dashboard is like the instrument panel of a car. The numbers update as you drive, so everyone can see the speed and the fuel without asking the mechanic.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a report you print once. It is a live view that people check every day.

skills.title: C Programming
skills.brief: C is the language closest to the hardware that's still widely used - the foundation of operating systems, firmware and embedded devices.

learn.detail: Types, functions, headers and how source becomes a binary.
Addresses, dereferencing and pointer arithmetic.
Contiguous memory and null-terminated strings.
malloc, free, and avoiding leaks and overflows.
Grouping data and mapping hardware registers.
Masks and shifts for setting and reading hardware bits.
Telling the compiler about hardware and read-only data.
gcc/clang, Makefiles, a debugger and compiler warnings.

skills.analogy: C is like working directly with the building's wiring and plumbing. You control every pipe, so you must check every joint yourself.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not an old language nobody uses. It runs operating systems and devices.

skills.title: Caching (Redis)
skills.brief: Caching keeps a copy of expensive results close at hand so they can be served instantly. Redis is the most widely used in-memory cache and data store.

learn.detail: Cut response times and database load for data that's read far more than written.
Browser, CDN, application memory, Redis, and the database itself.
Check the cache, fall back to the database, store the result.
TTLs, and clearing stale data when the source changes.
Cache-Control, ETags and what CDNs do with them.
Rate limiting, sessions, queues, leaderboards and pub/sub.
Stale data, cache stampedes and caching per-user data by mistake.

skills.analogy: A cache is the sandwich you prepared yesterday and kept in the fridge. It is quick to hand over, but you must throw it out when the ingredients change.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a copy you can trust forever. The hard part is knowing when to refresh it.

skills.title: CI/CD
skills.brief: Continuous integration and delivery: every change is automatically built, tested and deployed through a pipeline, so releases are frequent, small and boring.

learn.detail: Every push runs lint, type checks and tests automatically.
YAML workflows in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, versioned with the app.
Build once, deploy the same artefact everywhere.
Preview, staging and production - and promotion between them.
Store credentials safely; never echo them in logs.
Caching dependencies and running jobs in parallel.
Rolling, blue-green and canary releases, plus rollbacks.

skills.analogy: CI/CD is an assembly line with quality checks. Every change is built, tested and packaged automatically, so a good change reaches the shelf without anyone carrying it by hand.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not one tool. It is a pipeline that runs your checks on every change.

skills.title: Cloud Security
skills.brief: Keeping cloud accounts, identities, networks and data secure - least-privilege access, encryption, logging and catching misconfigurations before attackers do.

learn.detail: What the cloud provider secures, and what's on you.
Least privilege, roles over long-lived keys, MFA everywhere.
Private subnets, security groups and no unintended public exposure.
Encryption at rest and in transit; public bucket checks.
Secret managers instead of keys in code or environment files.
CloudTrail, GuardDuty-style alerts and who-did-what audit trails.
Benchmarks (like CIS) and automated misconfiguration scanning.

skills.analogy: Cloud security is like keys, badges and cameras for a building you rent. Each person gets only the keys they need, and every door is logged.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the cloud provider's job alone. You configure who can access what.

skills.title: Command Line & Linux Basics
skills.brief: The command line lets you control a computer by typing instead of clicking. Developers use it all day to run code, manage files, use Git and work on servers.

learn.detail: pwd, ls, cd - know where you are and move around the file system.
mkdir, touch, cp, mv, rm - create, copy, move and delete (carefully).
cat, less, head, tail -f - look inside files and follow logs as they grow.
grep and find - locate text in files and files on disk.
| > >> - chain small commands into powerful ones.
chmod, chown and sudo - who can read, write and run what.
ps, top, kill - see what's running and stop what's stuck.
PATH, environment variables and your shell config (.zshrc or .bashrc).

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education

skills.analogy: The command line is a kitchen where you call out exact instructions to the cook. The mouse is a menu with pictures, quick for a few dishes but slow when you need to repeat the same meal a hundred times.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a hacker tool. It is the most direct way to tell a computer what to do.

skills.title: C++
skills.brief: C++ gives programmers direct control over memory and performance. It powers game engines like Unreal, embedded systems, browsers, trading systems and much performance-critical software.

learn.detail: Types, functions, references and the compile–link process.
Stack vs heap, pointers, and why manual memory management is hard.
unique_ptr and shared_ptr - modern, safer ownership.
Constructors, destructors, copy and move semantics.
vector, map, string, algorithms and iterators.
Generic code, and reading template error messages.
CMake, compiler warnings, sanitizers and a debugger.
Cache-friendly data, avoiding copies and profiling.

skills.analogy: C++ is like a professional kitchen knife set. It is sharp and gives you exact control, but you must know how to hold each blade or you get cut.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just C with classes. It has its own large set of features and rules.

skills.title: C#
skills.brief: C# is a modern, typed language from Microsoft used for Unity games, .NET web services, desktop apps and enterprise systems.

learn.detail: Variables, methods, classes, structs and enums.
Classes, inheritance, interfaces and encapsulation.
Lists, dictionaries and querying data with LINQ.
Nullable reference types and avoiding null errors.
How Unity and .NET code is commonly structured.
Asynchronous code without blocking.
dotnet CLI, NuGet packages and project files.

skills.analogy: C# is a well-organised toolbox from Microsoft. It has tools for games, web services and desktop apps, all with the same labels and handles.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not only for Windows. It runs on other systems too.

skills.title: CSS
skills.brief: Paint, furniture, lighting - make the blueprint beautiful.

learn.detail: element, .class, #id, [attr], :hover, :focus, ::before - target any element
Every element = content + padding + border + margin. Understanding this unlocks all layouts.
display:flex - arrange children in a row or column. justify-content and align-items do most of the work.
display:grid - define rows AND columns. grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) makes three equal columns instantly.
@media (max-width: 640px) {} - change styles based on screen size. Mobile-first is the professional approach.
--brand-color: #7c6ee0 - define values once, use everywhere. Changing a theme becomes one line.
transition: all 0.2s ease - smooth property changes on hover. @keyframes for complex animations.
font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem) - text that scales perfectly between screen sizes without media queries.

skills.analogy: CSS is the interior design of a room. It decides the paint, the furniture's position and the lighting, but the walls (the HTML) must already be there.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a set of tricks to memorise. It is a system of rules that cascade from general to specific.

skills.title: Dart
skills.brief: Flutter's language - clean, null-safe, and fast to learn.

learn.detail: var for mutable variables. final = set once at runtime. const = compile-time constant. Prefer final.
String? name - the ? means this can be null. String name - this CANNOT be null. The compiler enforces this, preventing crashes.
void greet({required String name, int age = 0}) - named params make function calls readable: greet(name: 'Alex')
int double(int n) => n * 2 - single-expression functions use => instead of {} return. Same as JS.
Dart uses const constructors for immutable objects. class User { final String name; const User(this.name); }
List<String>, Map<String,int>, Set<int> - typed collections. Every item must match the type.
identical to JavaScript's async/await. Future = Promise. Stream = Observable (ongoing data).
extension on String { bool get isEmail => contains('@'); } - add methods to any existing class
mixin Serializable on Model { Map toJson() {...} } - share behaviour across classes without inheritance
Dart enums can have fields and methods - enum Status { active, inactive; bool get isActive => this==active; }

skills.analogy: Dart is like a clean, well-labelled toolbox for Flutter. It is designed to be easy to pick up and to keep tidy as a project grows.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not only for Flutter, but Flutter is where most people meet it.

skills.title: Data Modeling
skills.brief: Designing how data is organised into tables - facts, dimensions and keys - so it's correct, easy to query and consistent across reports.

learn.detail: One-to-many, many-to-many and keys.
Avoid duplicated data in transactional databases.
Fact tables (events) and dimension tables (who, what, where) for analytics.
Decide exactly what one row means - the most important modelling choice.
Track how attributes like a customer's plan change over time.
Define 'active user' once, in code, for everyone.

resources.title: dbt: How we structure our dbt projects

skills.analogy: Data modelling is designing the filing cabinet before you fill it. Each drawer holds one kind of thing, and labels link the drawers so you can find related papers.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not drawing diagrams for their own sake. A good model makes questions easy to answer.

skills.title: Data Storytelling
skills.brief: Turning analysis into a clear message that changes a decision - choosing the point, the right chart and the words around it.

learn.detail: What should the reader do or believe after this?
Put the takeaway in the title, not 'Revenue by month'.
Bars for comparison, lines for trends - and when not to use pie charts.
Remove gridlines, legends and colours that don't help.
Highlight the one thing that matters; grey out the rest.
Compared to what? How sure are we?
Situation, complication, resolution - or simply: what, so what, now what.

skills.analogy: Data storytelling is like a good guide on a tour. The guide picks which sights matter, in what order, and explains why each one is worth the walk.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not dumping every chart you made. It is choosing the one point that should change a decision.

skills.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
skills.brief: Ways to organise data (arrays, hash maps, trees, graphs) and step-by-step methods to solve problems efficiently. The core of most coding interviews.

learn.detail: Describe how time and memory grow with input size - O(1), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
Two pointers, sliding window and prefix sums - the most common interview patterns.
Constant-time lookups; the answer to a surprising number of problems.
Matching brackets, undo history, breadth-first search.
Pointers, reversal and fast/slow pointer tricks.
Binary trees, BSTs, DFS, BFS, and representing graphs as adjacency lists.
Top-k problems and priority queues.
Break problems into smaller ones and reuse answers.
Know the trade-offs, and binary search on answers, not just arrays.

skills.analogy: Data structures are the shelves and boxes in a warehouse. Choosing well means you find things fast. Algorithms are the routines a worker follows to sort and find things.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not memorising puzzles. It is choosing a sensible way to store and search data.

skills.title: Data Visualization
skills.brief: Turn numbers into insight anyone can see.

learn.detail: fig, ax = plt.subplots() - creates a figure and axes. fig.savefig('chart.png', dpi=150) to save it.
ax.bar(categories, values) - compare quantities across categories. Horizontal with barh() for long labels.
ax.plot(x, y, marker='o') - show trends over time. Multiple lines: call plot() again with a different series.
ax.scatter(x, y, c=color_col, alpha=0.6) - show relationships between two numeric variables.
ax.hist(data, bins=30, edgecolor='white') - show the distribution of a single numeric variable.
seaborn.boxplot(data=df, x='category', y='value') - show median, IQR, and outliers per group.
sns.heatmap(df.corr(), annot=True, cmap='coolwarm') - show correlations between all numeric columns.
sns.FacetGrid(df, col='category').map(sns.histplot, 'value') - the same chart repeated per category.
plt.style.use('dark_background'). seaborn.set_theme(style='whitegrid'). Always label axes and add titles.
px.bar(df, x='month', y='revenue', color='category') - hover-over data. For dashboards and presentations.

skills.analogy: A good chart is like a road sign. It tells the driver what matters in a glance, and a bad one is like a sign with too many words that nobody reads.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not making things look pretty. It is choosing the chart that answers the question.

skills.title: Data Warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake)
skills.brief: Cloud data warehouses store a company's analytical data and run SQL over billions of rows in seconds. BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift and Databricks are the most common.

learn.detail: Why analytics needs a different database from your app.
Why scanning a few columns of a huge table is fast.
Batch loads, ELT, and tools like Fivetran or Airbyte.
Organise tables so queries scan less data.
Pay-per-scan vs compute credits, and how to avoid surprise bills.
Roles, row- and column-level security for sensitive data.
Open table formats (Iceberg, Delta) and where they fit.

skills.analogy: A data warehouse is a giant organised storeroom for the whole company's records. Analysts can ask big questions across years of sales without touching the day-to-day shop.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the system that runs the app. It is where analysis happens, away from live traffic.

skills.title: dbt
skills.brief: dbt lets you transform data in your warehouse with version-controlled, tested SQL - bringing software engineering habits to analytics.

learn.detail: SELECT statements that become tables and views.
Build models on models, with a dependency graph.
unique, not_null, relationships and custom tests on your data.
Describe models and columns; generate a browsable site.
Declare raw data and load small reference tables.
Views, tables and incremental models.
Staging, intermediate and marts layers.

skills.analogy: dbt is like writing recipes for your data in SQL, with tests and version history. Each recipe is a step that turns raw ingredients into a clean table.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a database or a warehouse. It transforms data inside one.

skills.title: Deep Learning
skills.brief: Neural networks with many layers - the technology behind modern vision, speech and language models. Learn how they're built, trained and evaluated.

learn.detail: Linear layers, activations and how networks approximate functions.
Loss functions, backpropagation and optimisers like Adam.
Validation sets, regularisation, dropout and early stopping.
The building block of computer vision.
From RNNs to transformers.
Self-attention, embeddings and why they took over.
Start from a pretrained model instead of from scratch.

skills.analogy: Deep learning is like a factory line with many stations. Each station turns the raw input a little further, until the last one produces the answer.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a different kind of intelligence. It is machine learning with many layers.

skills.title: Deploying Web Apps
skills.brief: Getting your app from your laptop onto the internet - choosing a host, configuring environments and domains, and shipping updates safely.

learn.detail: Static hosts, platforms (Vercel, Netlify, Render, Fly.io) and raw cloud servers.
Separate config and secrets for development and production.
What happens at build time, and what runs on the server.
DNS records, custom domains and automatic certificates.
A live URL for every pull request.
Managed databases, migrations and backups.
Undo a bad release in seconds.
Principles for apps that deploy cleanly anywhere.

skills.analogy: Deploying an app is like opening a shop. You pick the building, connect the power and water, put up the sign with the right address, and open the doors.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not only uploading files. It includes domains, settings and a way to roll back.

skills.title: Design Systems
skills.brief: A shared set of design tokens, components and rules that keeps a product consistent and lets teams build faster. Engineers build and maintain the coded half.

learn.detail: Colours, spacing, type and radius as named variables.
Props that are flexible enough, but not so flexible everything looks different.
Buttons, dialogs and menus that are accessible by default.
Light, dark and brand themes from the same components.
Live examples and usage guidelines, often in Storybook.
Release changes without breaking every product that uses them.

skills.analogy: A design system is a shared set of building parts and rules, like the standard bricks and window sizes an architect uses on every building in a city.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a style guide PDF. It is working code and components that teams reuse.

skills.title: Developer Content & Speaking
skills.brief: Teaching developers through tutorials, docs, videos and talks - choosing the right format, making examples that actually work, and building a public body of work.

learn.detail: Tutorials teach, how-to guides solve, reference describes, explanations clarify.
Every code sample runs, from a clean start, exactly as written.
Get the reader to a working result as fast as possible.
Short, focused recordings with readable code and clear audio.
One idea per talk, a live demo with a backup, and slides that support you.
Answer questions publicly and turn repeated answers into content.
Completion, questions reduced and developer feedback - not just views.

skills.analogy: Developer content is like a guided walk through a museum. A good guide picks the highlights, explains them simply and tells you where to look next.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a list of links. It teaches one clear idea at a time.

skills.title: Docker
skills.brief: Docker packages an app with everything it needs into a container that runs the same on your laptop, a teammate's machine and in production.

learn.detail: An image is the recipe; a container is a running copy.
FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD - build your own images.
Order instructions so rebuilds are fast.
Multi-stage builds, slim base images and non-root users.
Expose services, persist data and pass configuration.
Run an app, its database and its cache together with one command.
Push and pull images from Docker Hub, GHCR or a cloud registry.
docker logs, docker exec and inspecting what went wrong.

skills.analogy: Docker is a shipping container for software. The app and everything it needs are packed inside, so it arrives and runs the same way on any ship or lorry.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a virtual machine. A container shares the host's operating system.

skills.title: Electronics Basics
skills.brief: The electronics an embedded engineer needs - voltage, current, resistance, reading schematics, using a multimeter and connecting sensors safely.

learn.detail: Ohm's law and what each one means in a circuit.
Resistors, capacitors, diodes, LEDs and transistors.
Symbols, nets and following a circuit on paper.
Building circuits without soldering.
Using a multimeter to check voltage, continuity and resistance.
Logic levels, pull-up resistors and ADCs.
Supplies, regulators and not frying your board.
Finding the pins, limits and timing you need.

skills.analogy: Electronics basics are like learning the plumbing of a house before fixing a tap. Voltage is the pressure, current is the flow, and resistance is the narrow pipe that slows it.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a full electronics degree. It is the part you need to read a circuit and use a multimeter.

skills.title: Embedded Protocols (UART, I2C, SPI, MQTT)
skills.brief: How chips, sensors and devices talk to each other - the wired buses inside a device (UART, I2C, SPI) and the messaging protocols that connect devices to the cloud (MQTT).

learn.detail: Simple serial communication - the debug console of most boards.
Two wires, many devices, addressed by number.
Faster, full-duplex communication with chip-select lines.
Clock polarity, phase and what the datasheet expects.
See exactly what's on the wire when things don't work.
Lightweight publish/subscribe messaging for IoT devices.
Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy and when to use each.

skills.analogy: Embedded protocols are the agreed sign language between chips and sensors. Each protocol sets how many wires there are, who speaks first and how messages are checked.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the internet protocol stack. These run inside one device on short wires.

skills.title: Flutter
skills.brief: Everything is a widget - UI, layout, animation, input, all of it.

learn.detail: A widget with no state - given the same inputs, always renders the same output. Text, Icon, Image are examples.
Has state that can change. When setState() is called, Flutter rebuilds only this widget and its children.
Column arranges children vertically. Row horizontally. Stack layers children on top of each other.
Inside Row/Column, Expanded fills remaining space. flex: 2 means 'take twice as much space as flex: 1'.
ListView.builder creates items lazily - only renders items on screen. Essential for long lists.
go_router package is the standard. Define routes as paths: '/home', '/profile/:id'. Navigate with context.go('/profile/1').
State management. Provider wraps the widget tree. Riverpod is the improved version - compile-safe, testable.
Builds different UI based on a Future's state: loading, success, or error. No manual setState needed.
Drive animations with a controller. Tween<double>(begin:0, end:1).animate(controller) - smooth value changes.
Call native iOS/Swift or Android/Kotlin code from Flutter when you need APIs Flutter doesn't expose.

skills.analogy: Flutter is like a painter's canvas where every screen is drawn from the same set of brushes. The same drawing looks the same on Android and iPhone.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a web framework. It builds apps for phones, desktop and the web from one codebase.

skills.title: Frontend Testing
skills.brief: Testing user interfaces the way people use them - components with Testing Library, and full flows in a real browser with Playwright.

learn.detail: Behaviour users see, not implementation details.
Render a component, interact with it, check the result - with Testing Library.
getByRole and getByLabelText before test IDs.
Test loading, success and error states without a real server (e.g. MSW).
Playwright drives a real browser through sign-up or checkout.
Catch layout regressions and a11y issues automatically.
Avoid flaky waits; run tests in CI on every pull request.

skills.analogy: Frontend tests check the interface the way a customer uses it. It is like a mystery shopper who walks in, orders, and checks the bill is right.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not checking the code line by line. It checks what the user sees and can do.

skills.title: Maths for Games
skills.brief: The maths behind movement, cameras, collisions and physics in games - vectors, trigonometry, matrices and a little calculus, learned visually and applied in code.

learn.detail: Position, direction and velocity; adding, scaling and normalising.
Angles, facing direction and surface normals.
Sine and cosine for rotation, circles and waves.
Local, world and screen space.
Translation, rotation and scale combined.
Lerp, easing and smooth camera movement.
Bounding boxes, circles and raycasts.
Velocity, acceleration, gravity and frame-rate independence.

resources.title: 3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development (free online)

skills.analogy: Game maths is the geometry that tells a character how to turn, how far to jump and whether the ball hit the wall. It is the map behind every move on screen.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not advanced physics. It is mostly vectors and angles.

skills.title: Git & GitHub
skills.brief: Git records every change to your code so you can undo mistakes, work on ideas in parallel, and collaborate without overwriting each other. GitHub is where teams share it.

learn.detail: git init, git add, git commit - save snapshots of your project with clear messages.
git log, git diff, git restore and git revert - see what changed and safely go back.
git switch -c feature - work on something new without touching the main code.
Combine branches, and resolve conflicts calmly when two changes touch the same lines.
git clone, git push, git pull - sync your work with GitHub.
Propose changes, get reviews, and merge - the way almost every team works.
Keep node_modules, build output and .env files out of the repo. Never commit keys.
Tidy a branch before merging - and know when not to rewrite shared history.

skills.analogy: Git is like a notebook where every page is dated and you can tear out a bad page or copy it to try a different idea, without losing the rest.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a backup folder. It is a record of every change, with who made it and why.

skills.title: Go
skills.brief: Go is a simple, fast, compiled language built at Google. It's the language of much cloud infrastructure - Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform are all written in Go.

learn.detail: Variables, functions, structs, slices and maps.
if err != nil - explicit error handling instead of exceptions.
Small, implicit interfaces that make code easy to test.
go mod, imports and project layout.
Goroutines, channels, select and sync primitives.
net/http, encoding/json, context and testing - often enough on their own.
go test, table-driven tests and benchmarks.
Single static binaries that are easy to ship.

skills.analogy: Go is like a well-run delivery service: simple rules, fast handovers, and many workers moving at once. It was made so large teams can build and run big systems without confusion.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a scripting language. It compiles to fast programs.

skills.title: GraphQL
skills.brief: GraphQL is an API style where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request, described by a typed schema.

learn.detail: The contract between client and server.
Ask for exactly the fields you need, nested, in one round trip.
Create, update and delete through the same endpoint.
Server functions that fetch each field's data.
Batching with DataLoader so nested queries don't hammer the database.
Apollo Client, urql or Relay for caching on the frontend.
Great for many clients and complex data; REST is often simpler.

skills.analogy: GraphQL is like ordering from a menu where you choose exactly which parts of each dish you want, in one order, instead of asking for the whole dish each time.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a replacement for every API. It trades simplicity for flexibility.

skills.title: How the Internet Works
skills.brief: What actually happens between typing a web address and seeing a page - DNS, IP addresses, HTTP requests and responses, and how browsers turn code into pixels.

learn.detail: A browser (client) asks; a server answers. Everything on the web is this conversation.
DNS turns codejourney.space into an IP address, like a phone book for the internet.
Methods (GET, POST), status codes (200, 404, 500), headers and bodies.
How encryption keeps data private in transit, and why the padlock matters.
HTML becomes the DOM, CSS styles it, JavaScript changes it, and the browser paints pixels.
Why the second visit is faster, and how content is served from near the user.
Read the Network tab to see every request a page makes.

resources.title: Cloudflare Learning Center: What is DNS?

skills.analogy: The internet is like the postal service. A web address is the address on the envelope, DNS is the directory that finds the right building, and the page is what comes back in the reply.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not one big computer somewhere. It is many machines passing messages to each other.

skills.title: HTML
skills.brief: The skeleton of every webpage - structure without style.

learn.detail:
–

,

,

, , , - the vocabulary of HTML
href, src, alt, class, id - extra information attached to tags
<header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <footer> - tags with meaning
<form>, <input>, <button>, <select>, <textarea> - how users send data
,
The browser turns your HTML into a tree of objects - JS reads and changes this tree

skills.analogy: HTML is the skeleton of a page. It decides where the head, the arms and the text go, before any clothes or colour are added.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the design. Colour and layout come from CSS.

skills.title: Incident Response & On-call
skills.brief: What to do when production breaks - detecting it, coordinating a calm response, restoring service fast, and learning from it with blameless post-mortems.

learn.detail: Alerts on user-facing symptoms, so you hear about problems before customers do.
Agree in advance what counts as SEV1 vs SEV3 and who gets paged.
Incident commander, communications lead and responders.
Roll back, fail over or switch off a feature - find the root cause later.
Status updates for users and stakeholders on a regular rhythm.
Step-by-step guides for known failures.
Timeline, contributing factors and action items - without blaming people.
Rotations, handovers and reducing noisy alerts.

skills.analogy: Incident response is like a fire drill for a building. Everyone knows who calls the fire service, who guides people out, and who checks the cause afterwards.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not finding someone to blame. It is restoring service and learning from what happened.

skills.title: Internal Developer Platforms
skills.brief: Internal developer platforms give engineers self-service golden paths - create a service, deploy it, observe it - so product teams ship without each solving infrastructure from scratch.

learn.detail: Treat developers as users: research, roadmap and adoption metrics.
Opinionated, well-supported defaults for the common case.
Scaffold a new service with CI, observability and deploys built in.
Catalogues, docs and self-service actions (e.g. Backstage).
Declarative deployments reconciled from Git (Argo CD, Flux).
Security and cost policies enforced by the platform, not by tickets.
Lead time, deploy frequency, onboarding time and developer satisfaction.

skills.analogy: An internal developer platform is a self-service vending machine for engineers. They press a button for a new service, and the platform sets up the database, the pipeline and the dashboards.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a single product you buy. It is the set of paved paths your company builds for its engineers.

skills.title: Tech Interviewing
skills.brief: How tech hiring actually works - résumés, coding rounds, system design, behavioural questions and offers - and how to prepare for each without burning out.

learn.detail: Screens, technical rounds, onsite loops and how decisions are made.
Impact-focused bullet points and projects that prove skills.
Think aloud, clarify, start simple, test your code.
Requirements first, then trade-offs - for mid-level and above.
Prepare stories with the STAR format: situation, task, action, result.
SQL for data, take-homes for frontend, troubleshooting for DevOps.
Practise out loud with another person.
Compare total compensation and negotiate respectfully.

skills.analogy: A tech interview is like a driving test. Knowing how to drive matters, but so does showing the examiner you can do the manoeuvres they ask for, under time pressure.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a trick quiz. It tests how you think out loud as much as the answer.

skills.title: JavaScript
skills.brief: The brain - makes pages think, respond, and come alive.

learn.detail: const, let (not var). Types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, object, array, symbol.
Regular: function greet(name){…} Arrow: const greet = (name) => 'Hello '+name. They're the same but arrow functions have no own 'this'.
document.querySelector('#btn') gets the element. .textContent, .style, .classList let you change it. This is the core skill.
addEventListener('click', fn) - user clicks, scrolls, types, hovers. Your code runs in response.
.map(), .filter(), .reduce(), .find(), .some() - transform data without loops. The backbone of modern JS.
const {name, age} = user - extract values in one line. const [first, ...rest] = arr - same for arrays.
fetch('/api/data') returns a Promise. async/await makes it read like synchronous code without blocking the browser.
try { await fetch(url) } catch(err) { handle gracefully } - always handle what can go wrong.
import {greet} from './utils.js' - split code into files. export makes functions available to other files.
A function that 'remembers' the variables from where it was created, even after that scope is gone. Counters and event handlers use this constantly.

skills.analogy: JavaScript is the staff of a restaurant. HTML is the menu on the wall and CSS is the decor. JavaScript takes the orders, reacts when someone taps a button and updates what the guest sees.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the same as Java. The names are close, but the languages are different.

skills.title: Jetpack Compose
skills.brief: Jetpack Compose is Android's modern way to build interfaces in Kotlin - you describe what the screen should look like for a given state, and Compose keeps it up to date.

learn.detail: @Composable functions that describe UI from data.
Column, Row, Box, LazyColumn and modifiers for spacing and size.
remember, mutableStateOf and why the UI redraws when state changes.
Keep state in the caller so composables stay reusable and testable.
Hold screen state that survives rotation; collect StateFlow safely.
Navigation Compose for moving between screens with arguments.
Colours, typography, dark mode and dynamic colour.
LaunchedEffect and friends for loading data and one-off events.
@Preview for fast iteration and Compose UI tests.

skills.analogy: Jetpack Compose is like describing a screen as a recipe. You say what the screen should look like for a given state, and the phone builds it.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not the old XML layout style. It is the modern way to write Android screens.

skills.title: Kotlin
skills.brief: Android's official language - concise, safe, Jetpack Compose.

learn.detail: val = immutable (like final). var = mutable. Prefer val everywhere. The compiler warns you when you don't need var.
String? = nullable. String = cannot be null. ?. for safe access. ?: for default. !! forces non-null (use rarely).
data class User(val name: String, val email: String) - auto-generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy()
fun String.isEmail() = contains('@') - add methods to any class, even standard library ones
suspend fun load() { val data = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { api.fetch() } } - async without callbacks
Flow<T> is Kotlin's Stream - emit multiple values over time. Collected in a coroutine. Used for real-time UI.
@Composable fun ProfileCard() - declarative UI like Flutter. States drive re-composition automatically.
Survives screen rotations. Holds UI state. Exposes StateFlow that Compose collects and re-renders on change.
@Entity, @Dao, @Database - SQLite with type safety and coroutine support. The standard local persistence library.
Dependency injection via annotations. @Inject, @HiltViewModel - Hilt provides instances; you declare what you need.

skills.analogy: Kotlin is a modern, tidy version of the language Android was built on. It has the same bones, with fewer ways to trip over yourself.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a separate platform. It runs on Android and the Java virtual machine.

skills.title: Kubernetes
skills.brief: Kubernetes runs and manages containers across many machines - restarting failures, scaling with traffic and rolling out updates without downtime.

learn.detail: What it solves - and when a simpler platform is the better choice.
How your containers are run and kept alive.
Stable networking inside the cluster and traffic from outside.
Configuration without rebuilding images.
Fair scheduling and avoiding noisy neighbours.
Liveness and readiness probes.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, rolling updates and rollbacks.
Day-to-day commands and packaging apps.

skills.analogy: Kubernetes is the harbour master for containers. It decides which ship goes where, replaces a sinking one, and adds more ships when the port gets busy.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not something a small app needs. It pays off when many containers run across many machines.

skills.title: Linux Administration
skills.brief: Running and looking after Linux servers - users, packages, services, logs and security. Most of the internet runs on Linux, so this is the base of every infrastructure role.

learn.detail: /etc, /var/log, /home, /usr - where things live and why.
Who can do what, sudo, and least privilege.
apt or dnf - installing, updating and pinning software.
systemctl start/enable/status, and reading journalctl logs.
top, htop, free, df, du - what's using CPU, memory and disk.
Key-based login, config files and hardening a server.
ip, ss, curl, dig - check ports, connections and DNS.
ufw or firewalld, and keeping a server patched.

skills.analogy: Linux is the engine room of most servers on the internet. Running it well is like keeping a ship's engine running: regular checks, clear logs and a plan for when something fails.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just a desktop. Most of its use is on servers, where it runs quietly.

skills.title: LLM APIs
skills.brief: Calling large language models from code - sending messages, controlling output, handling streaming, tools and errors - through provider APIs like Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic.

learn.detail: System instructions, user and assistant turns, and conversation history.
Model choice, max tokens and temperature - and what they change.
Ask for JSON that matches a schema, and validate it.
Show tokens as they arrive for a responsive UI.
Let the model request actions your code performs.
Count tokens, cache prompts and pick model sizes sensibly.
Rate limits, retries with backoff and timeouts.
Keep API keys on the server; never in the browser.

skills.analogy: Calling an LLM API is like placing an order with a very capable assistant by phone. You send the request in a fixed format and get a reply back, and you handle the case where the line drops.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not running the model yourself. The provider hosts it and bills per use.

skills.title: LLM Evaluation
skills.brief: Measuring whether an LLM feature actually works - building test sets, scoring outputs with code, people and other models, and catching regressions before users do.

learn.detail: Without measurement, every prompt change is a guess.
Read real outputs and categorise failures before writing metrics.
Representative examples, edge cases and past failures.
Format, length, required facts and forbidden content.
Using a model to grade - with a clear rubric and checks against human labels.
When people need to judge, and how to make it consistent.
Run them on every change and track scores over time.

skills.analogy: Evaluating an LLM feature is like tasting a dish before it leaves the kitchen, every time the recipe changes. You need a fixed set of test dishes, not one lucky taste.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not checking one good answer. It is measuring many answers against the same tests.

skills.title: Machine Learning
skills.brief: Teaching computers to find patterns humans can't see.

learn.detail: A mathematical function that maps inputs (features) to outputs (predictions). You train it on historical data to learn the mapping.
Train on 80%, evaluate on the held-out 20%. Testing on training data is cheating - the model memorised it. NEVER do this.
The model memorised the training data too well - 98% accuracy in training, 60% on new data. Reduce complexity or add more data.
Predict a continuous number (house price, sales amount). Assumes a linear relationship between features and target.
Predict a category (spam/not spam, churn/retain). Despite the name, it's a classification algorithm.
A tree of if-then rules learned from data. Interpretable. Random Forest = hundreds of trees voting together (more accurate).
Regression: MAE, RMSE, R². Classification: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC. Choose the metric that matches your business goal.
Transform raw data into informative features. Normalise numeric features. Encode categoricals. Remove correlated features. This is 80% of the work.
Split data into 5 folds, train/test 5 times on different splits. The average score is much more reliable than one train/test split.
Automatically try all combinations of hyperparameters and return the best. Pass param_grid={'n_estimators':[100,200], 'max_depth':[3,5,7]}.

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Intro to Machine Learning

skills.analogy: Machine learning is like teaching a child to spot dogs by showing many photos and correcting mistakes, rather than writing a rule for every breed.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not magic or thinking like a person. It finds patterns in examples.

skills.title: Maths for Machine Learning
skills.brief: The maths machine learning is built on - linear algebra, calculus and probability - at the level you need to understand models, not to prove theorems.

learn.detail: Data as vectors, models as matrix operations, dot products as similarity.
What a layer in a neural network actually computes.
How a small change in input changes output - the heart of training.
How gradients flow backwards through layers (backpropagation).
Random variables, distributions, expectation and Bayes' rule.
Gradient descent, learning rates and why training sometimes diverges.
Finding the directions that matter most in data.

skills.analogy: This maths is the toolbox behind a machine learning model. You do not need to build every tool yourself, but you should know what each one is for and when it breaks.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a pure maths degree. It is the maths you use to read and tune models.

skills.title: Message Queues & Events
skills.brief: Message queues and event streams let services hand off work and react to events without waiting on each other - the backbone of background jobs and scalable systems.

learn.detail: Move slow work (emails, video processing, reports) out of the request path.
Who sends, who receives, and what sits in between.
RabbitMQ/SQS-style work queues vs Kafka-style event logs.
At-least-once delivery, and why consumers must be idempotent.
What happens to messages that keep failing.
When order matters and how streams preserve it.
Publishing events so other services can react independently.

skills.analogy: A message queue is like a takeaway order ticket rail. The counter writes a ticket and moves on, and the kitchen works through the tickets at its own pace.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a direct phone call. The sender does not wait for the reply.

skills.title: Microcontrollers (Arduino, ESP32, STM32)
skills.brief: Microcontrollers are tiny computers on a single chip. Programming them means working with GPIO pins, timers, interrupts and peripherals - with kilobytes of memory.

learn.detail: Reading buttons and driving LEDs and relays.
Precise timing, dimming LEDs and controlling motors.
Reacting to events immediately, and keeping handlers short.
Reading analogue sensors.
UART, I2C and SPI hardware blocks.
Fitting in flash and RAM; sleep modes for battery life.
Serial logging, debuggers (SWD/JTAG) and logic analysers.
Arduino for learning, ESP32 for Wi-Fi projects, STM32 for industry.

resources.title: Embedded Systems – Shape the World (free course)

skills.analogy: A microcontroller is a tiny computer on a single chip, like the brain inside a washing machine. It reads its sensors, runs a fixed program and switches its outputs.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a laptop in a small box. It has very limited memory and power.

skills.title: MLOps
skills.brief: The practices and tools for getting ML models into production and keeping them healthy - reproducible training, deployment, monitoring and retraining.

learn.detail: Version data, code and parameters so any model can be rebuilt.
Log runs and compare them with MLflow or Weights & Biases.
Promote models from staging to production with approvals.
Batch predictions vs real-time APIs, and latency budgets.
Data drift, prediction drift and business metrics after launch.
Automate training on schedules or triggers.
Test data and models, not just code.

skills.analogy: MLOps is the kitchen operations behind a restaurant. Recipes are versioned, dishes are repeatable, and someone watches the fridge temperature so the food stays safe after it leaves the kitchen.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just training a model once. It keeps a model working in production.

skills.title: Mobile App Testing
skills.brief: Testing mobile apps at every level - unit, widget/component and end-to-end on real devices - so releases don't crash on the phones your users actually have.

learn.detail: Business logic tested without any UI.
Render a screen in isolation and interact with it.
Drive the real app on an emulator or device.
Screen sizes, OS versions and low-end Android phones.
Test offline, slow and error responses.
Automated builds and tests for both platforms.
Firebase Crashlytics or Sentry to catch what tests miss.

skills.analogy: Mobile testing is like test-driving a car on real roads, in the rain and on bad fuel. A test in a simulator is useful, but real phones find problems the simulator misses.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not running the app once on your own phone. Phones differ in size, speed and OS version.

skills.title: Networking
skills.brief: How computers find and talk to each other - IP addressing, DNS, TCP, HTTP, load balancers and firewalls - and how to debug it when they can't.

learn.detail: A practical view of the OSI/TCP-IP model - what lives where.
IPv4, CIDR notation (10.0.0.0/16) and private vs public addresses.
Record types (A, CNAME, MX, TXT), TTLs and propagation.
Connections, ports, handshakes and when each is used.
Certificates, termination and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 basics.
Layer 4 vs layer 7, reverse proxies like Nginx.
Allowing only the traffic you mean to.
ping, traceroute, dig, curl -v, ss and tcpdump.

skills.analogy: Networking is the road system between houses. Addresses tell you where each house is, the roads carry the traffic, and traffic lights and gates control who can pass.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not only Wi-Fi. It covers how any two machines find and reach each other.

skills.title: Next.js
skills.brief: Next.js is the most popular React framework. It adds routing, server rendering, data fetching and API routes, so you can build fast, search-friendly full-stack apps.

learn.detail: Folders become URLs; layouts wrap pages.
Render on the server by default; opt into the browser with 'use client'.
Pre-render pages at build time, or render per request when you must.
Fetch on the server, and understand how Next.js caches and revalidates.
Build API endpoints and form submissions inside the same app.
Titles, descriptions, sitemaps and Open Graph images per page.
next/image and next/font for fast, stable pages.
Vercel or any Node host - and environment variables done safely.

skills.analogy: Next.js is a ready-made kitchen for React. Someone has already set up the stoves, the storage and the delivery, so you can focus on the dishes.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a separate language. It is React with routing, server rendering and data built in.

skills.title: Node.js
skills.brief: JavaScript on the server - APIs, databases, authentication.

learn.detail: The most popular Node.js framework. Create routes with app.get('/path', handler). Middleware for auth, logging, parsing.
GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE. Return JSON. Use HTTP status codes (200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 500).
Functions that run between request and response: authenticate user, parse JSON body, log requests, validate inputs.
Prisma ORM gives you type-safe database access. Define your schema once, get auto-generated, type-checked queries.
JSON Web Tokens - sign a token on login, verify it on every protected request. Never store plain passwords.
.env files keep secrets (DB passwords, API keys) out of your code. Never commit them to git.
Global error middleware catches unhandled errors. Never expose stack traces to users in production.
Railway (backend + DB) or Render for hosting. Vercel for frontend. Environment variables set in the dashboard.

skills.analogy: Node.js lets JavaScript work in the back kitchen as well as at the counter. The same staff can take orders, check the stock and send the bill.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a separate framework. It is a runtime that runs JavaScript on a server.

skills.title: Observability
skills.brief: Logs, metrics and traces that let you understand what a system is doing in production - so you notice problems before users do and find the cause quickly.

learn.detail: Logs (events), metrics (numbers over time) and traces (a request's journey).
JSON logs with request IDs you can search and correlate.
Latency, traffic, errors and saturation - the four golden signals.
Follow one request across services with OpenTelemetry.
Grafana or a hosted tool showing health at a glance.
Alert on user-facing symptoms, not every blip; avoid alert fatigue.
Define 'reliable enough' and measure against it.
Tools like Sentry for exceptions with full context.

resources.title: Google SRE book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

skills.analogy: Observability is the dashboard and warning lights of a car. Logs, metrics and traces tell you the speed, the temperature and the engine noise, so you notice a fault before the car stops.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just logging. Logs are one of three signals.

skills.title: OWASP Top 10
skills.brief: The OWASP Top 10 is the industry's standard list of the most critical web application security risks - the shared vocabulary of application security.

learn.detail: Users acting outside their permissions - the most common serious flaw.
Sensitive data exposed through weak or missing encryption.
SQL, command and other injection - including cross-site scripting.
Flaws baked into the design that no code fix can fully patch.
Default settings, verbose errors and open cloud storage.
Outdated libraries with known vulnerabilities.
Weak passwords, broken sessions and credential stuffing.
Untrusted updates, missing monitoring and server-side request forgery.

skills.analogy: The OWASP Top 10 is the shared list of the most common ways a house gets broken into. Every builder should know it, like the basic locks everyone checks.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a complete list of every risk. It is the most common ones to check first.

skills.title: NumPy & Pandas
skills.brief: The engine that makes Python fast enough for real data.

learn.detail: np.array([1,2,3]) - like a list but typed and fast. Supports element-wise operations without loops.
array * 1.08 multiplies every element. array[array > 100] filters without a loop. This is the core NumPy pattern.
pd.read_csv('data.csv') loads it. df.head() shows first 5 rows. df.info() shows types. df.describe() shows statistics.
df['column'] for a series. df[['a','b']] for multiple columns. df.loc[row,col] for labels. df.iloc[0,0] for positions.
df[df['sales'] > 100] - boolean mask. df.query('sales > 100 and region == "North"') - readable string syntax.
df.groupby('category')['amount'].agg(['mean','sum','count']) - summarise by category in one line.
pd.merge(customers, orders, on='customer_id', how='left') - same as SQL LEFT JOIN. Combine related DataFrames.
df.isnull().sum() - count NaNs per column. df.dropna() removes rows. df.fillna(0) replaces NaN with zero.
df['name'].apply(str.upper) - apply any function to a column. .map() for Series, .apply() for row/column-level.
Convert string dates to datetime objects. Then df['date'].dt.month, dt.year, dt.day_name() give time features.

skills.analogy: Pandas is a spreadsheet inside Python. You can sort, filter and join whole tables with one line of code instead of clicking through thousands of rows.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a database. It works on data that is already loaded into memory.

skills.title: Performance Testing
skills.brief: Load and stress testing - simulating many users to find how much traffic a system handles, where it slows down and how it fails.

learn.detail: Load, stress, spike and soak tests - and what each answers.
Model real user journeys and traffic patterns.
Throughput, latency percentiles (p95, p99) and error rate.
Pass/fail criteria tied to real requirements.
Correlate load with CPU, memory, database and logs.
k6, JMeter and Locust.
Never load-test production without permission and a plan.

skills.analogy: Performance testing is like filling a bus with passengers to see how many it can carry before it slows down or breaks.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a test of one fast user. It checks what happens under many users at once.

skills.title: Playwright
skills.brief: Playwright automates real browsers - Chromium, Firefox and WebKit - for reliable end-to-end tests, with auto-waiting, tracing and parallel runs built in.

learn.detail: npm init playwright, then a test that visits a page and checks it.
getByRole, getByLabel and getByText - resilient, user-facing selectors.
expect(...).toBeVisible() instead of sleeps.
Reuse login state and test data.
Mock or intercept API calls for stable tests.
UI mode, trace viewer, screenshots and videos.
Run across browsers and shards in CI.
Organise large suites without hiding what tests do.

skills.analogy: Playwright is a robot shopper that uses a real browser. It clicks, types and checks what appears, the way a customer would, and waits for the page to be ready before each step.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a browser extension. It drives real browsers from code.

skills.title: PostgreSQL
skills.brief: PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database and the most-used database among developers. Learn it beyond basic SQL: schemas, indexes, transactions and performance.

learn.detail: Tables, primary and foreign keys, constraints and normalisation.
Text, numeric, timestamps with time zones, JSONB, arrays and UUIDs.
B-tree indexes, when they help, and reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
ACID, isolation levels and avoiding race conditions.
Changing schemas safely on a live database.
Roles, grants and row-level security.
pgvector for embeddings, PostGIS for maps, pg_stat_statements for tuning.
Point-in-time recovery and connection pooling.

skills.analogy: PostgreSQL is a sturdy filing cabinet with strict rules about what can go in each drawer. It can also hold shapes of data the cheaper cabinets cannot.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just a place to store text. It enforces rules about the data it holds.

skills.title: Prompt Engineering
skills.brief: Writing instructions that get reliable, useful results from language models - clear goals, context, examples and output formats - and testing that they work.

learn.detail: State the task, the audience and what a good answer looks like.
Include the information the model needs instead of hoping it knows.
Show one or two input/output pairs for tricky formats.
Separate instructions, context and data with clear sections or tags.
Ask for JSON or a fixed template when code will read the result.
Ask for step-by-step thinking on complex tasks when appropriate.
Change one thing at a time and measure on a fixed set of examples.

skills.analogy: Writing a prompt is like briefing a new contractor. The clearer the goal, the context and an example of good work, the less time you spend fixing the result.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a secret phrase that unlocks the model. It is clear instructions.

skills.title: Python
skills.brief: The language of data science - readable, fast to write, faster to run with libraries.

learn.detail: Python is dynamically typed - no type declarations. int, float, str, bool, None. Use type hints for clarity.
[1,2,3] for ordered collections. {'name':'Alex','age':30} for key-value pairs. Both mutable.
[x*2 for x in data if x>0] - filter and transform in one readable line. Faster than a for loop.
def clean(text): return text.strip().lower(). Lambda: lambda x: x*2. Lambdas for simple one-line transforms.
name="Alex"; print(f"Hello {name}") - embed expressions in strings. Cleaner than concatenation.
with open('data.csv') as f: - automatically closes the file even if an error occurs. Always use with open().
Use sparingly. You'll mostly use library classes (DataFrame, Model). Know how to read class docs though.
python -m venv venv → source venv/bin/activate → pip install pandas. Never install packages globally.
.ipynb files. Mix code, output, and text. The standard for exploratory analysis and sharing results.
def process(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series: - hints don't enforce types but make code readable and IDE-friendly.

skills.analogy: Python is like a clear recipe book written in plain language. It is easy to read, so the cook can focus on the food.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not slow for everything. Heavy number work is done by libraries written in faster languages.

skills.title: PyTorch
skills.brief: PyTorch is the most widely used deep learning framework in research and industry - tensors, automatic gradients and building blocks for training neural networks.

learn.detail: Multi-dimensional arrays on CPU or GPU.
Automatic gradients for any computation.
Define models from layers.
Forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimiser step.
Batching, shuffling and loading data efficiently.
Moving models and data to a device; mixed precision.
Checkpoints and exporting models for serving.

skills.analogy: PyTorch is a workbench for building and testing neural networks. You can open the parts, change one and see what happens, which suits researchers well.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a model you download. It is the framework you write models with.

skills.title: R
skills.brief: Built by statisticians, for statisticians - the academic standard.

learn.detail: c(1,2,3) is a vector. data.frame() is R's DataFrame. tibble() from tidyverse is cleaner.
data |> filter() |> group_by() |> summarise() - chain operations left-to-right. Identical mental model to Python method chaining.
filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by(), summarise(), arrange(), join_left() - equivalent to Pandas operations.
pivot_wider() and pivot_longer() - reshape data between wide and long format. Essential for visualisation.
ggplot(data, aes(x=month, y=revenue)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + theme_minimal() - layered grammar of graphics.
t.test(), chisq.test(), aov(), lm() - native R has every statistical test you'll ever need.
model <- lm(salary ~ years_exp + education, data=df) - formula syntax. summary(model) gives coefficients, p-values, R².
Mix R code, output, and prose in one document. Knit to HTML, PDF, or Word. The standard format for reproducible research.
Build interactive web dashboards entirely in R - sliders, dropdowns, reactive charts. No JavaScript needed.
The R ecosystem for genomics and bioinformatics - 2,000+ packages for biological data analysis.

skills.analogy: R is a specialist toolbox that statisticians built for their own work. It has a tool for almost every kind of test and chart they might need.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not only for academics. Many analysts use it in industry too.

skills.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
skills.brief: RAG lets a language model answer from your own documents: retrieve the most relevant passages, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer - with citations.

learn.detail: Models don't know your private or recent data; retrieval gives it to them at question time.
Split documents into passages that keep their meaning - by heading, not every 500 characters.
Turn text into vectors so similar meanings sit close together.
Vector search, keyword search (BM25) and hybrid search.
Re-score the top results for relevance before sending them to the model.
Instruct the model to answer only from context and cite sources.
Measure retrieval quality and answer faithfulness separately.
Re-index changed documents automatically.

skills.analogy: RAG is like an open-book exam. Before answering, the model looks up the right pages from your notes and answers from them, rather than from memory.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not training the model on your documents. The documents are looked up at question time.

skills.title: React Native
skills.brief: If you know React, you're 70% of the way to mobile.

learn.detail: The native equivalents of div, p, img. View is a container. Text renders text (must be inside Text component). Image for local or remote images.
