CSS-like but camelCase. No cascade, no inheritance. Inline styles are allowed but StyleSheet.create is preferred for performance.
All Views are flex containers by default. flexDirection: 'column' is the default (opposite of web). Layouts work the same as CSS Flexbox.
The performant equivalent of HTML table or map() rendering. Only renders visible items. Use this for any list of items.
The correct way to handle taps. Replace touchables with Pressable - it supports complex press states and accessibility.
The standard navigation library. Stack navigator, Tab navigator, Drawer navigator. Navigate with navigation.navigate('Profile', { id: 1 })
@react-native-async-storage/async-storage - key-value store that persists between app launches. Use for tokens, preferences.
Build React Native apps without Xcode or Android Studio. Expo Go app lets you preview instantly on your phone. expo-camera, expo-location, etc.
const isDark = useColorScheme() === 'dark' - detect the user's system theme and apply the right colours.
Modern RN uses JSI (JavaScript Interface) for direct JS-to-native calls without the asynchronous bridge. Much faster.

skills.analogy: React Native is like a translator who lets you speak React to a phone. Your components become real phone screens, so the React skills carry over.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a web view wrapped in an app. It uses the phone's own buttons and lists.

skills.title: React
skills.brief: Build UIs like LEGO - components you assemble, not HTML you repeat.

learn.detail: Function components are the only way. They take props, return JSX. Think of them as custom HTML tags.
<UserCard name='Alex' role='admin' /> - pass data into a component like HTML attributes
const [count, setCount] = useState(0) - when state changes, React re-renders only the affected component
Runs after render. Use for: fetching data, subscriptions, DOM manipulation. Cleanup with return fn.
Holds a value across renders without causing re-renders. Also the way to access actual DOM elements.
Prevent expensive recalculations and function re-creation on every render. Use when profiling shows slowness.
Share state globally without prop-drilling. createContext → Provider wraps the tree → useContext reads it.
<BrowserRouter> → <Routes> → <Route path='/about' element={<About/>}/> - client-side navigation
Server state management. Handles caching, background refetching, loading/error states for you.
Controlled: value={state} onChange={setState}. Uncontrolled: useRef. React Hook Form for complex forms.

skills.analogy: React is like building with LEGO. You make small pieces, each with its own job, and snap them together into a whole screen. When one piece changes, only that piece is rebuilt.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a full framework for everything. It handles the interface, and other tools handle routing and data.

skills.title: REST APIs
skills.brief: REST APIs let apps talk to servers over HTTP using URLs, methods and JSON. Almost every app - web, mobile or AI - is built on top of them.

learn.detail: Model things as nouns: /users, /users/42/orders.
GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE removes.
200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 401/403 auth errors, 404 Not Found, 500 server error.
Content-Type, Authorization, and consistent response shapes.
Reject bad input early with clear error messages.
?page=2&limit=20&sort=-created - keep responses small and predictable.
Change APIs without breaking clients; describe them with OpenAPI.
fetch, curl and tools like Postman or Bruno.

skills.analogy: A REST API is a well-organised counter at a shop. You ask for a thing by its name (a URL), say what you want to do (GET, POST), and get a receipt back in a standard format (JSON).
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a single fixed product. It is a style of building web services that many systems share.

skills.title: Real-Time Operating Systems
skills.brief: Real-time operating systems such as FreeRTOS and Zephyr let embedded devices run several tasks with predictable timing - essential when a deadline missed is a failure.

learn.detail: Hard vs soft deadlines and predictability over raw speed.
Priorities, pre-emption and the scheduler.
Mutexes, semaphores and avoiding priority inversion.
Queues, event groups and notifications between tasks.
Ticks, delays, software timers and interrupt interaction.
Static vs dynamic allocation and stack sizing.
Tracing tools and finding deadlocks and stack overflows.

resources.title: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real Time Kernel (book)

skills.analogy: An RTOS is like a train timetable. Each task gets its slot on time, so the important jobs always run when they must, even when many things are happening.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a fast operating system for desktops. It is built for predictable timing.

skills.title: Security Testing (SAST, DAST, Pentesting)
skills.brief: Finding vulnerabilities before attackers do - with automated scanners in the pipeline and hands-on testing of running applications.

learn.detail: Static analysis scans source code for risky patterns (Semgrep, CodeQL).
Catch vulnerable packages and leaked keys automatically.
Dynamic scanning probes a running app from the outside (OWASP ZAP).
Intercept and modify requests with Burp Suite to test logic flaws.
Separate real, exploitable issues from false positives.
Clear reproduction steps, impact and a recommended fix.
Only test with written permission; respect scope.

skills.analogy: Security testing is hiring a friendly burglar to try the doors and windows, along with automatic scanners that check the locks every day.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a single scan. It combines automated checks with hands-on testing.

skills.title: Shell Scripting (Bash)
skills.brief: Writing Bash scripts to automate repetitive tasks - deployments, backups, setup and glue between tools. The everyday language of infrastructure work.

learn.detail: #!/usr/bin/env bash, making files executable, and running them.
Always quote "$vars" - the source of most Bash bugs.
if, case, for and while for real automation.
set -euo pipefail, and checking that commands succeeded.
$1, $@, getopts - build small reusable tools.
grep, sed, awk, cut, sort and jq for JSON.
cron and systemd timers.
ShellCheck catches mistakes before they bite.

resources.title: Missing Semester: Shell tools and scripting

skills.analogy: A shell script is a recipe card for the terminal. You write the steps once, and the computer repeats them exactly, instead of you typing the same commands every morning.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a full programming language for large projects. It is best for gluing tools together.

skills.title: Apache Spark
skills.brief: Apache Spark processes data too large for one machine by spreading the work across a cluster, with SQL and DataFrame APIs in Python (PySpark).

learn.detail: When data or computation outgrows a single machine.
Familiar operations that run in parallel.
Transformations build a plan; actions run it.
Why some operations are expensive and how to reduce them.
Parquet and Delta/Iceberg tables for fast analytics.
Caching, broadcast joins and reading the Spark UI.

skills.analogy: Spark is like a large kitchen with many cooks. A huge order is split into parts, each cook handles a part, and the results are combined into one meal.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not needed for small data. A single laptop is faster for a file that fits in memory.

skills.title: Spreadsheets
skills.brief: Excel and Google Sheets are still the most-used data tools in business. Analysts are expected to clean, summarise and chart data in them quickly and accurately.

learn.detail: One header row, one record per row, consistent types - the basis of everything else.
SUM, AVERAGE, COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, IF and text functions.
XLOOKUP (or INDEX/MATCH) to join data from two tables.
Summarise thousands of rows by category in seconds.
Pick the right chart and label it clearly.
Remove duplicates, split columns, fix dates, TRIM stray spaces.
Repeatable cleaning steps in Excel.
Totals that reconcile, and spotting obviously wrong numbers.

skills.analogy: A spreadsheet is a ledger with a calculator built in. It is the first tool most people use to check a total, sort a list or make a quick chart.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a database. Once data grows, it becomes hard to trust in a spreadsheet alone.

skills.title: SQL
skills.brief: The language every database speaks - non-negotiable for data roles.

learn.detail: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE department = 'Engineering' ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 10
COUNT(*), SUM(amount), AVG(score), MAX(date), MIN(price) - collapse many rows into one summary row
GROUP BY category - split rows into groups, then aggregate each group. WHERE filters before grouping, HAVING after.
INNER JOIN - only matching rows. LEFT JOIN - all left rows + matches. Use ON to specify the join condition.
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE country = 'India')
WITH monthly AS (SELECT ...) SELECT * FROM monthly - name a subquery and reference it. Essential for readability.
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY sales DESC) - analytics without collapsing rows. The senior analyst skill.
DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at), EXTRACT(year FROM date), date + INTERVAL '7 days' - work with time data
CASE WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A' WHEN score >= 80 THEN 'B' ELSE 'C' END - conditional column values
COALESCE(value, 0) returns first non-null. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for filtering. NULLIF(a, b) returns null if a=b.

skills.analogy: SQL is how you ask a librarian for exactly the books you want: by author, by year, grouped by genre. The librarian finds them without you walking the shelves.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a spreadsheet formula. It runs against whole databases of tables.

skills.title: State Management
skills.brief: Deciding where data lives in an app and how it changes - local component state, shared state, and server data that needs caching and syncing.

learn.detail: useState for things only one component cares about.
Move state to the nearest common parent when two components share it.
Compute values from state instead of storing copies that drift.
Share rarely-changing values (theme, current user) without prop drilling.
Data from APIs needs caching, refetching and loading states - TanStack Query handles this.
Zustand or Redux Toolkit when many distant parts of the app share changing state.
Filters, tabs and search queries often belong in the URL.

skills.analogy: State is the memory of an app. It is like the order slip on the kitchen rail: everyone needs to read the same slip, and changing it in one place must update every station.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not something to put everywhere. Keep state close to where it is used, and share only what must be shared.

skills.title: Statistics
skills.brief: The maths behind why your conclusions are actually true.

learn.detail: Mean, median, mode, variance, std deviation, skewness. df.describe() gives all of these for a DataFrame.
Normal (bell curve), Poisson (rare events), Binomial (yes/no trials). Knowing which distribution fits your data matters.
Take enough samples and their means will be normally distributed - even if the original data isn't. The foundation of inference.
H₀ (null: no difference) vs H₁ (alternative: there is a difference). p-value < 0.05 means reject H₀.
Comparing means of two groups. scipy.stats.ttest_ind(group_a, group_b) - are these groups statistically different?
Testing if two categorical variables are related. Are conversion rates different by device type?
df.corr() shows correlation. But correlation ≠ causation. Ice cream sales correlate with drowning rates (both increase in summer).
A result can be statistically significant but practically meaningless. Cohen's d measures how large the real difference is.
'95% CI: [12.3, 18.7]' - we're 95% sure the true value is in this range. More informative than just the mean.
Assign users randomly to control/treatment, measure the metric, run a t-test. Minimum sample size matters - calculate it first.

skills.analogy: Statistics is like a taste test. One spoonful is not enough to judge a whole pot, so you need to know how many spoonfuls, and how much they vary, before you trust the verdict.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just averages. It is how sure you can be about what the numbers show.

skills.title: Swift
skills.brief: Apple's language - the only way to deeply build for iPhone.

learn.detail: let = constant (can't change). var = variable. Swift's type inference means you rarely need to write the type explicitly.
var name: String? = nil - the ? marks a value as possibly absent. Unwrap with if let name { } or name ?? default.
Structs are value types (copied on assignment) - prefer them. Classes are reference types (shared). Use classes for identity.
Like interfaces. protocol Identifiable { var id: UUID { get } }. A type that 'conforms to' a protocol must implement it.
func first<T>(_ array: [T]) -> T? { return array.first } - write once, works for any type
{ (x: Int) -> Int in return x * 2 } - blocks of code you pass around. Shorthand: { $0 * 2 }
Declarative UI like Flutter. @State drives re-renders. VStack, HStack, ZStack for layout. Previews in Xcode.
Swift's concurrency model. func loadData() async throws { let user = try await api.fetchUser() }
@Observable marks a class; @State/@Binding drives SwiftUI re-renders. The equivalent of Flutter's setState + ChangeNotifier.
Apple's local persistence. SwiftData (iOS 17+) is the modern approach: @Model class Post {}. Automatically persistent.

skills.analogy: Swift is the language of the Apple kitchen. It is designed for the iPhone, Mac and iPad, with the tools already laid out for you.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not Objective-C with a new name. It is a separate, modern language.

skills.title: SwiftUI
skills.brief: SwiftUI is Apple's modern framework for building interfaces on iPhone, iPad, Mac and Watch - declarative views that update automatically when your data changes.

learn.detail: Small structs that describe UI, styled with chained modifiers.
VStack, HStack, ZStack, Grid, List and ScrollView.
@State for local values, @Binding to share them, @Observable models for app data.
NavigationStack, sheets and passing data between screens.
Load data with async/await and .task; show loading and error states.
SwiftData for storing data on the device.
VoiceOver labels and text that scales.
#Preview for fast iteration; wrap UIKit when you need it.

skills.analogy: SwiftUI is like describing a screen with simple building blocks. You say what should show, and Apple's system keeps it up to date when the data changes.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a drag-and-drop tool. You write the screen in code.

skills.title: System Design
skills.brief: How to design software that serves many users reliably - splitting work across services, databases, caches and queues, and choosing trade-offs you can defend.

learn.detail: Clarify users, scale, read/write ratio and what 'fast enough' means before drawing boxes.
Vertical vs horizontal scaling, load balancers and stateless services.
SQL vs NoSQL, indexes, replication, sharding and when you actually need them.
What to cache, where (CDN, application, database) and how to keep it fresh.
Queues and events for slow jobs like email, video processing and notifications.
CAP in practice, idempotency, retries and what happens when a service is down.
Logs, metrics and traces so you know when the design is failing.
Back-of-the-envelope maths for traffic, storage and bandwidth.

skills.analogy: System design is planning a restaurant before it opens: how many tables, how many cooks, where the storage goes, and what happens on the busiest Friday night.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not drawing boxes for an interview. It is deciding how a system behaves under real load and failure.

skills.title: Tailwind CSS
skills.brief: Tailwind CSS is a utility-first framework: you style elements with small classes like 'flex gap-4 text-lg' instead of writing separate CSS files. Fast, consistent and very popular.

learn.detail: Spacing, colour, typography and layout as small composable classes.
md:, lg: - mobile-first breakpoints right in the markup.
hover:, focus-visible:, disabled:, dark: - without writing selectors.
Define colours, fonts and spacing once; use them everywhere.
Flexbox and Grid utilities for real page layouts.
Extract components, not @apply everywhere.
Tailwind is CSS - specificity, the cascade and layout still matter.

skills.analogy: Tailwind is like a set of spice jars. You add small ready-made flavours directly to the dish, instead of writing a new recipe for every seasoning.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a component library. It is a set of small style classes you apply yourself.

skills.title: Technical Writing
skills.brief: Writing clearly about technical work - READMEs, pull requests, design docs and incident reports - so others can understand, review and build on it.

learn.detail: Write for the person who'll read it: a reviewer, a new teammate, or a non-technical manager.
Put the conclusion or request first, then the details.
What it is, how to run it, how to contribute - in that order.
What changed, why, how to test it, and anything risky.
Problem, options considered, decision and trade-offs.
Short sentences, real examples, no filler.
A simple box-and-arrow diagram often replaces three paragraphs.

skills.analogy: Technical writing is like giving directions to a friend who is new to the city. You name the landmarks in order and skip the things they do not need to know yet.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not writing a long essay. It is writing so the next person can act on it without asking you.

skills.title: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform)
skills.brief: Describing servers, networks and databases in code instead of clicking in a console - so infrastructure is reviewable, repeatable and recoverable. Terraform (and OpenTofu) is the most widely used tool.

learn.detail: Review changes like code, recreate environments, and avoid configuration drift.
Describe AWS, GCP, Azure or Cloudflare resources in HCL.
See exactly what will change before it changes.
What Terraform remembers, remote state and locking.
Reuse code across dev, staging and production.
Package common patterns (a VPC, a service) for reuse.
Running plans in CI and applying through reviewed pull requests.

skills.analogy: Terraform is a written blueprint for a building. Instead of building by hand and forgetting what was done, you describe the result and the tool builds it the same way every time.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a script that runs once. It keeps the real setup matching the description.

skills.title: Test Automation
skills.brief: Building and maintaining automated test suites that run on every change - choosing tools, keeping tests fast and stable, and making failures easy to understand.

learn.detail: Repetitive, high-value, stable checks - not everything.
Balance unit, API and end-to-end tests.
Playwright, Cypress and Selenium - strengths and trade-offs.
Find and fix the root causes: timing, shared data, order dependence.
Seed data, isolated environments and cleanup.
Run on pull requests, shard for speed, publish reports.
Readable tests, shared helpers and code review for test code.

skills.analogy: Test automation is a robot that repeats the same checklist after every change, so a human only looks at the surprises.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a replacement for thinking about tests. Automation runs the checks you designed.

skills.title: Test Design & Strategy
skills.brief: Deciding what to test and how - finding the cases most likely to break, choosing the right level of test, and writing bug reports people can act on.

learn.detail: Turn acceptance criteria into concrete test cases.
Group inputs that behave the same; test one from each group.
Bugs cluster at edges: 0, 1, max, max+1.
Empty, too long, wrong type, duplicate, concurrent.
Structured, time-boxed exploration guided by risk.
Test what matters most to users and the business first.
Steps to reproduce, expected vs actual, environment and evidence.
What to automate, at which level, and what to monitor in production.

resources.title: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level syllabus

skills.analogy: Test design is choosing which doors to check in a building. You pick the ones most likely to be left unlocked, not every window in the place.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not writing as many tests as possible. It is writing the ones that matter most.

skills.title: Testing Basics
skills.brief: Writing code that checks your code. Tests catch bugs before users do, let you change things without fear, and document how the code is meant to behave.

learn.detail: Fast feedback, safe refactoring and living documentation.
Test one function or module in isolation with clear inputs and expected outputs.
Check that pieces work together - your API with a real database, for example.
Drive the real app like a user would; fewer, slower, but high confidence.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a handful of end-to-end tests.
A simple structure that keeps tests readable.
Replace slow or external dependencies - sparingly.
Tests only protect you if they run on every change.

skills.analogy: Tests are the checklist a pilot runs before take-off. Each check is quick, and together they catch the problem before the plane is in the air.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not proof that code is perfect. It shows the cases you thought of still work.

skills.title: Threat Modeling
skills.brief: Thinking through how a system could be attacked before it's built - what you're protecting, from whom, and which defences matter most.

learn.detail: What are we building? What can go wrong? What will we do about it? Did we do a good job?
Draw components, data stores and trust boundaries.
Spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.
What's valuable, and who realistically wants it.
Likelihood and impact - fix what matters first.
Map each threat to a control: auth, validation, encryption, rate limiting, logging.
Lightweight threat models in design reviews, not a one-off document.

skills.analogy: Threat modelling is walking around your house before you move in and asking where a burglar would try first, and which valuables matter most.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a one-off form. It is a way of thinking you repeat as the system changes.

skills.title: TypeScript
skills.brief: JavaScript with a safety net - catches bugs before they run.

learn.detail: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, void - annotate any variable or parameter
string[] or Array<string> - typed arrays. [string, number] - tuple with fixed positions
interface User { id: number; name: string } - define the shape of any object
type Role = 'admin' | 'viewer' - the value can only be one of these exact strings
function getFirst<T>(arr: T[]): T - write code that works for any type but stays safe
const name = 'Alex' - TypeScript already knows this is a string. You don't need to write the type.
name?: string - optional property. readonly id: number - can't be changed after creation
Partial<User>, Omit<User,'id'>, Pick<User,'name'> - transform types without repeating yourself

skills.analogy: TypeScript is like a spell-checker that runs before you send the email. It warns you about a mistake before the reader sees it.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a different browser language. It compiles down to plain JavaScript.

skills.title: UI & UX Design Basics
skills.brief: The design fundamentals every interface builder needs - hierarchy, spacing, typography, colour, usability and working in Figma - so what you build is clear and pleasant to use.

learn.detail: Size, weight, colour and position tell people what matters first.
Consistent spacing scales and grids make interfaces feel calm.
Readable sizes, line lengths and a small type scale.
A limited palette, accessible contrast and colour with meaning.
Feedback, consistency, error prevention and recognition over recall.
Map the steps a person takes to finish a task, and remove the unnecessary ones.
Frames, auto layout, components and inspecting designs as a developer.
Follow Material and Apple guidelines where users expect them.

skills.analogy: UI design is like arranging a shop window. You decide what catches the eye first, what sits together, and what the passer-by should do next.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not decoration. It is about making the next action clear.

skills.title: Unity
skills.brief: Unity is the most widely used game engine for mobile and indie games, scripted in C#. It handles rendering, physics, audio and publishing to many platforms.

learn.detail: Scenes, GameObjects, components and the Inspector.
MonoBehaviour, Update, FixedUpdate and the component model.
Rigidbodies, colliders, triggers and raycasts.
The Input System and responsive character controllers.
Menus, HUDs and scaling across screen sizes.
Reusable objects and data-driven design.
Bringing a game to life.
Publishing to PC, mobile and web; finding performance problems.

skills.analogy: Unity is a stage crew for games. It handles the lights, the physics and the sound, so the game designer can focus on what happens in the scene.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a game on its own. It is the engine you build games in.

skills.title: Vector Databases
skills.brief: Vector databases store embeddings and find the most similar ones fast - the search engine behind semantic search, recommendations and RAG.

learn.detail: What a vector represents and how embedding models create them.
Cosine similarity, dot product and distance.
HNSW and IVF indexes trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed.
Search only within a user's documents or a date range.
Combine vectors with keyword search for better results.
pgvector in Postgres, or dedicated stores like Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate or Chroma.

skills.analogy: A vector database is like a library where books are shelved by meaning, not by title. You can ask for "books like this one" and get the close matches quickly.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not a normal database with a faster search. It finds the nearest meanings.

skills.title: Web Animation & Interaction
skills.brief: Using motion to make interfaces feel responsive and understandable - CSS transitions, keyframes, the Web Animations API and motion libraries - without hurting performance or accessibility.

learn.detail: Show cause and effect, guide attention and smooth changes in state.
Animate between states on hover, focus and class changes.
Multi-step animations with @keyframes.
Natural easing curves and durations that feel quick, not sluggish.
Animate transform and opacity; avoid layout-triggering properties.
The Web Animations API and libraries like Motion for gestures and layout animation.
Animate between pages and states with the View Transitions API.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion for people who need less movement.

resources.title: An Interactive Guide to CSS Transitions

skills.analogy: Good motion is like a door that swings shut slowly instead of slamming. It tells the person what just happened, without shouting for attention.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not animation for its own sake. Motion should explain a change, not distract.

skills.title: Web Performance
skills.brief: Making pages load fast and respond instantly - especially on mid-range phones and slow networks - measured with Core Web Vitals.

learn.detail: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness) and CLS (visual stability) - what they measure and good targets.
Lighthouse, Chrome DevTools Performance panel and real-user data.
Ship less JS: code splitting, lazy loading and server rendering.
Modern formats, correct sizes, lazy loading and font-display.
Cache headers and serving from near the user.
Avoid layout thrashing and long tasks that block input.
Set a performance budget and check it in CI.

skills.analogy: Web performance is like keeping a shop's queue short. The customer should be served quickly on a slow connection, not only on a fast one.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not just making images smaller. It covers how the page loads, how it responds and how it moves.

skills.title: Web Security Basics
skills.brief: The common ways web apps get attacked - injection, cross-site scripting, broken access control and more - and the habits that prevent them.

learn.detail: The industry's list of the most critical web application risks.
SQL and command injection - always use parameterised queries.
Escape output and use a Content Security Policy.
Check permissions server-side on every request.
SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens for state-changing requests.
Keep keys out of code and out of the browser bundle.
Keep packages updated and watch for known vulnerabilities.
HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options and friends.

skills.analogy: Web security is like locking doors, checking the ID of every delivery and not leaving the spare key under the mat. Most break-ins happen through the easy mistakes.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not one tool you install. It is a set of habits applied everywhere.

skills.title: Working with Customers
skills.brief: The skills that make engineers effective in front of customers - discovering the real problem, scoping what to build, communicating trade-offs and building trust.

learn.detail: Ask about past behaviour and real pain, not hypothetical wishes.
Let the customer explain their process before proposing a solution.
Turn a big ask into a small first version that proves value.
Describe technical choices in terms of time, cost and risk.
Show working software early; tailor it to the audience.
Be clear about what you will and won't deliver, and by when.
Turn patterns across customers into clear product requests.

resources.title: How to talk to users (YC Startup Library)

skills.analogy: It is like a good waiter who asks what the guest actually wants before bringing the dish. Engineers who do this build the right thing faster.
skills.whatItIsNot: It is not only for sales. It is how engineers learn what problem to solve.
